P22 (S3 file store) code slice landed — bucket names de-hardcoded, Minio client made region-aware, EnsureBucketAsync tolerant of a least-privilege denial, CSP media-src added, nginx recordings proxy made cloud-safe. DEF-015 was under-scoped: it named three recording handlers, but Topics/AttachFileToTopic.cs carried a FOURTH const ('acmp-topics'), a bucket no AWS environment provisions and which the app IAM cannot create — topic attachment would have failed outright in cloud. All four now read StorageOptions (Storage:RecordingsBucket / Storage:AttachmentsBucket); defaults reproduce the on-prem MinIO split so nothing moves, and both cloud services point at the single per-env bucket. U1's offline half is answered and PINNED BY TEST rather than by a spike run: Minio 6.0.3 recognises any Amazon host and substitutes its own region map (AWSS3Endpoints), so us-east-1 is addressed as s3.amazonaws.com path-style regardless of the configured ACMP_S3_ENDPOINT — the CSP media-src origin therefore had to be s3.amazonaws.com, and getting that wrong would have blocked playback silently with nothing in the API logs. Reading the SDK also showed PutObjectPartAsync issues an AbortMultipartUpload on a part-count mismatch for known-size streams (every upload we make) while 03-iam.sh granted no s3:AbortMultipartUpload — added to both policy documents before P20 is ever run, so it is a script edit rather than a live IAM change. DEVIATION from the slice text, recorded not silent: the nginx /acmp-recordings/ proxy is neutralized (variable upstream + resolver, so nginx stops resolving 'minio' at config load and the cloud web container boots) rather than deleted, because deleting it would regress the on-prem/ngrok dev playback path that deploy/.env actually uses and force a second nginx template ahead of P25. NOT DONE, and not claimed: AC-078 and AC-083 both need a live bucket and stay Pending; no AWS call was made; the AWSSDK.S3 fallback was not built. P22 follow-up: the nginx leg was asserted before it was verified, and verifying it found a real break. Rendering the template in the pinned nginx-unprivileged image proved BOTH halves of the recordings-proxy deviation mechanically — with keycloak/api resolvable and NO minio host the committed template passes `nginx -t`, while restoring the literal `proxy_pass http://minio:9000;` fails with `[emerg] host not found in upstream "minio"`, so the variable+resolver form is load-bearing rather than cosmetic. The first verification run was itself wrong, though: it mounted the template into the BASE image, which substitutes every defined env var, whereas Dockerfile.web pins NGINX_ENVSUBST_FILTER to KEYCLOAK_ORIGIN alone. CI caught it (acmp-web-1 exited 1 on the e2e stack). A template variable missing from that filter is not left harmlessly alone: the surviving ${ACMP_MEDIA_ORIGIN} is then read by nginx as one of its OWN runtime variables and the config dies at load with `unknown "acmp_media_origin" variable`. Fixed by listing it in the filter regex with an empty default in the image, and re-verified as UID 101 in all three combinations (old filter reproduces the CI failure; new filter renders `media-src 'self' ;` when empty and `media-src 'self' https://s3.amazonaws.com` when set). Lesson for any future CSP source added to the template: the envsubst filter must be extended in the same edit.

P23 (backup / restore / DR) code slice landed, and the drill earned its keep. backup.sh now backs up BOTH stateful databases (Acmp + keycloak, which ADR-0036 put on the same instance), WITHOUT the WITH COMPRESSION clause that SQL Server Express rejects outright, and copies the .bak files to S3 as a hard requirement rather than a best-effort leg. The pg_dump and mc-mirror legs are gone — Keycloak has no Postgres, and mirroring an S3 bucket onto a 4 GiB instance would be copying AWS's own durability into the thing you are protecting against. restore.sh's Keycloak leg piped a gzipped pg_dump into psql inside a container ADR-0036 DELETED, written to fail non-fatally: it could only ever have reported a successful restore of a system nobody can log into. It now restores keycloak as a SQL database, resolves every .bak before touching any of them, and stops only the dependents actually running (SINGLE_USER alone is a race — the api reconnects and takes the single-user slot). THREE FAILED DRILL RUNS, each worth the time: (1) MSYS rewrote the in-container /opt/mssql-tools18 path to C:/Program Files/Git/opt/... — a Windows harness artifact, not a script bug; (2) the same again because the gate suppressed its own output, so the gate was changed to print the failure — a gate that cannot say why it failed is not a gate; (3) the real one, DEF-017: SQL Server writes the .bak ITSELF as uid 10001 while Docker had created the bind mount root-owned 0755, so BACKUP died with 'Operating system error 5(Access is denied.)'. That would have failed identically on the EC2 host, at 02:00, in a cron log, while the deployment looked backed up. backup.sh now preflights the mount and names the fix. Also added: 02-s3.sh expires CURRENT versions on the backups bucket ONLY (recordings never expire) — uncompressed nightly backups for two databases would otherwise grow without bound on an account whose budget actions cut access at 100% and stop instances at 120%. Evidence: U4 gate PASSES unattended — 3 -> 0 -> 3 on keycloak, Express, no COMPRESSION, Keycloak healthy after its database was restored (16 passed / 1 failed overall). NOT DONE and not claimed: the S3 upload leg and the Acmp-database half of AC-080 need a live environment; AC-080 stays Pending. P24 part 1 (image publish) landed on feat/p24-cd-pipeline. Two pieces: deploy/aws/06-github-oidc.sh registers GitHub's OIDC provider and a push-only ECR role, and ci.yml gains a `publish` job. The identity choice is the substance — the obvious route is an IAM user with an access key in GitHub secrets, and that is deliberately refused: such a key never expires, every workflow in the repo can read it, and it outlives the machine it was pasted from; this project lost three keys to a temp file earlier the same day. The trust policy is scoped to one repository and to refs/heads/main, refs/tags/* and environment:*, so a fork pull request mints a token whose `sub` matches nothing and cannot push to the registry the servers pull from. Permissions are push+read on acmp/* only — no DeleteRepository, no BatchDeleteImage, no lifecycle writes, because CI publishes images but must not be able to remove the one production is running. The publish job sits INSIDE ci.yml rather than in its own workflow because `needs` is the only gate that makes publishing an untested commit structurally impossible; a separate workflow would trigger on workflow_run and re-derive the head SHA, which is more machinery for a weaker guarantee. id-token: write is per-job so the test jobs cannot mint an AWS token. api/worker/sqlserver-fts build once (environment-agnostic, promoted by digest); web builds twice as <sha>-uat and <sha>-prod because ADR-0037 bakes VITE_OIDC_AUTHORITY in, and the two are never interchangeable. Both authorities are REQUIRED repository variables rather than defaulted — a wrong or empty authority ships a bundle that cannot log in and fails in the browser with nothing in the API logs, the same silent-failure shape as the P22 CSP media-src bug. Digests are recorded to a 90-day artifact because promotion deploys by digest, so what UAT tested and what production runs are the same bytes rather than the same label. The job is guarded by vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN != '' so that merging it before the role exists leaves main green instead of red, and setting the variable switches it on with no follow-up commit. NOT DONE, NOT CLAIMED: 06-github-oidc.sh has NEVER BEEN RUN — the AWS session expired mid-slice, so the provider, role and policy do not exist and the publish job has never executed; nothing here is verified beyond YAML/shell parse. DRIFT RECORDED: SL-024 says the digest artefact is 'consumed by promote.sh', but promote.sh is the P18b on-prem warm-standby VM failover script (restore a backup, bring the stack up, stop before DNS cutover) whose premise — a standby VM — does not exist in the cloud topology. Image promotion needs its own script; this is the same class of stale assumption as P23's restore.sh pointing at a container ADR-0036 deleted.

P24 part 1 VERIFIED LIVE. PR #166 squash-merged as 9739632; the publish job ran for the first time and succeeded, and the five images exist in ECR (api 104 MB, worker 100 MB, sqlserver-fts 1.41 GB, web -uat and -prod 22.9 MB each). The digest artifact matches `aws ecr describe-images` on all five, so promotion-by-digest has real bytes to point at. The substantive check was NOT the green tick. The claim that mattered is ADR-0037's premise that the two web images are not interchangeable, and the tempting proof — the two digests differ — is unsound: Docker builds are not reproducible by default, so differing digests are equally consistent with the build-arg being silently ignored. ECR's compressed sizes actively misled in the other direction, reporting the PROD image 5 bytes LARGER although its authority URL is 4 characters SHORTER. The sound test was to open the bundle: the top layer of each web image was pulled via get-download-url-for-layer and grepped. The UAT image contains only https://uat.acmp.anas7ammo.dev/kc/realms/acmp, the PROD image only https://acmp.anas7ammo.dev/kc/realms/acmp, neither contains the other's, and the UNCOMPRESSED dist differs by exactly 4 bytes — precisely len('uat.'). Per-environment baking is therefore evidenced, not inferred. Two pre-merge suspicions were checked rather than assumed and both were already correct: ecr:DescribeImages IS in the role policy, so the Record-digests step did not 403 after five successful pushes; and the LIVE trust policy really is narrowed to the single subject repo:A-H-911/acmp:ref:refs/heads/main, because 06-github-oidc.sh is written idempotently (it branches on get-role and calls update-assume-role-policy when the role exists) and was re-run after db7f47c — a create-only script would have left that narrowing on paper. Coupling to protect: the trust matches :ref:refs/heads/main, so if anyone ever adds an `environment:` key to the publish job, GitHub mints sub=repo:...:environment:NAME, which matches nothing and fails at assume-role rather than anywhere that reads like the cause. NOT DONE, NOT CLAIMED: no image has been RUN anywhere. Pull-and-boot on a real instance is entirely unproven and belongs to P25; publishing bytes is not the same as those bytes starting. NEW FINDING (cost): there is no ECR lifecycle policy, and the CI role deliberately cannot create one (ecr:PutLifecyclePolicy is excluded on purpose, correctly). Every push to main therefore adds an immutable SHA tag that nothing ever reaps. Shared layers keep the marginal cost per merge small, but the growth is unbounded against a $60/mo budget and needs an operator-run lifecycle policy. NEW FINDING (governance): SL-024 has NO acceptance criterion. AC-075..AC-085 bind to SL-020/021/022/023/025/026/027; the CD slice alone has none, so its exit is unmeasurable and this verification had no criterion to be recorded against. Surfaced to the operator rather than self-issued, because adding an AC moves the acceptance denominator. TOOLING: GNU tar treats a C:/ path as a remote host spec (host:path, rmt) and tried to network-connect to a host named 'C'; --force-local or a POSIX path is required. That failure was masked by a 2>/dev/null on the verification step and produced an EMPTY grep result, which was one careless sentence away from being reported as 'the authority is not baked in' — a fabricated defect. Suppressing stderr on a check converts a broken check into data-shaped output.

CORRECTION to PE-142, plus two fixes. (1) PE-142's cost finding — 'there is no ECR lifecycle policy' — was WRONG, and was asserted without reading 04-ecr.sh. The script has applied one since P20 (`put-lifecycle-policy`, keep last 10, re-applied idempotently on every run) and `aws ecr get-lifecycle-policy` confirms it live on all four repositories. Retracted. Checking it did surface the REAL defect underneath, which is sharper than the false one: the rule counts IMAGES (`imageCountMoreThan`), and `web` is the only repository receiving TWO images per merge (<sha>-uat and <sha>-prod, because ADR-0037 bakes the authority in). A flat keep-10 therefore gave web FIVE commits of rollback depth against ten for api/worker/sqlserver-fts. That asymmetry fails precisely where it matters, because promotion deploys BY DIGEST: rolling back roughly six merges would find api and worker present and the matching web images already expired — a partial rollback missing the one image that carries the environment identity. 04-ecr.sh now expresses retention in COMMITS (KEEP_COMMITS=10) and scales the image count per repository, and the corrected 20-image policy was applied live to acmp/web. (2) U3's Arabic CONTAINS() gate, which failed all four runs on 2026-08-03 and was recorded as undiagnosed, is DIAGNOSED and FIXED — and it was never flaky. The populate-crawl poll called FULLTEXTCATALOGPROPERTY('ftc','PopulateStatus') WITHOUT a `USE ftsspike` prefix, and sq() connects with no -d, so it executed in master. Full-text catalogs are scoped to the current database (CREATE FULLTEXT CATALOG: 'unique among all catalog names in the current database'; both Microsoft examples for the function prefix USE <database>), so in master the catalog does not exist, the function returned NULL, and `${pst:-1}` masked NULL as 'still populating'. The loop therefore never broke: the 'wait for the crawl' was a blind 45-second sleep that observed nothing, after which CONTAINS simply RACED the populate. That is exactly why it passed on an idle machine and failed on a loaded one — the gate never had a readiness signal at all. Every OTHER statement in the block carries an explicit USE; this one line was the sole omission. Secondary defect found in the same place: PopulateStatus is deprecated, and Microsoft warns that looping on the CATALOG-level property 'takes CPU cycles away from the database and full-text search processes, and causes timeouts', directing callers to the table-level property. The poll now asks OBJECTPROPERTYEX(OBJECT_ID('dbo.t'),'TableFulltextPopulateStatus') in the right database, treats a NULL/non-numeric read as LOUD ('!') rather than indistinguishable from 'busy', and reports a crawl that never reaches idle instead of silently handing CONTAINS a race. NOT CLAIMED: the fix is reasoned + syntax-checked (bash -n) but has NOT been re-run — Docker Desktop is not running in this session, and re-running the spike is the operator's call. The diagnosis stands on the code and the vendor documentation; the green re-run does not yet exist. (3) AC-086 created to close the governance gap PE-142 raised: SL-024 was the only PH-5 slice with no acceptance criterion, so its exit was unmeasurable. Recorded Met on the live evidence as AV-087.

U3 poll hardened again after review caught a REGRESSION in the first fix — recorded because the near-miss is the useful part. PE-144's replacement gated on OBJECTPROPERTYEX(...,'TableFulltextPopulateStatus') = 0. That is wrong in a way that reads correct: status 0 means 'no population in progress', which is ALSO true BEFORE the crawl has started, and CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ... WITH CHANGE_TRACKING AUTO queues the crawl asynchronously — the DDL returns before the FTS host picks up the work. The loop could therefore read 0 on its FIRST iteration, break in under a second, and hand CONTAINS the identical race it was written to remove. On a fast or idle machine that is strictly WORSE than the 45-second blind sleep it replaced, because the old code at least burned real time the crawl could use. Same defect class as the original bug: a readiness signal that is not evidence of readiness. The gate now reads BOTH properties as 'status:itemcount' and breaks only on idle AND at least one row indexed — TableFulltextItemCount is documented as 'the number of rows that were successfully full-text indexed', so it asserts the row is actually searchable rather than that the server is merely quiet. '0:0' is now explicitly the not-started state and is NOT success; a NULL/empty read (wrong database or missing object) stays LOUD. Verified by exercising the state machine over 0:0, 0:1, 1:0, empty, NULL and 9:3 — only 0:<non-zero> breaks. STILL NOT RE-RUN: Docker Desktop is not running in this session, so U3 remains DIAGNOSED and HARDENED, not proven. The single assertion the whole gate now rests on — that TableFulltextItemCount reaches >=1 on this box once the crawl lands — is exactly the one that cannot be obtained from the code, and it needs a live run in the isolated `acmpspike` project. Do not let 'diagnosed' become 'fixed' in a later summary without a green run.

U3 CLOSED — root-caused, fixed, and re-run GREEN (17 passed / 0 failed). The Arabic CONTAINS() gate was never flaky; it was three stacked defects, and finding each one required fixing the instrumentation that was hiding the next. (1) The populate poll queried FULLTEXTCATALOGPROPERTY without `USE ftsspike`, and sq() connects with no -d, so it ran in master where the catalog does not exist; NULL came back, `${pst:-1}` masked it as 'still populating', and the wait degenerated into a blind 45-second sleep that observed nothing before CONTAINS raced the crawl. (2) The first replacement gated on TableFulltextPopulateStatus = 0 — wrong in a way that reads correct, because 0 also means 'the crawl has not started', and CHANGE_TRACKING AUTO queues it asynchronously, so the loop could break on iteration one and reproduce the race FASTER than the original bug. Caught in review before it shipped. (3) The second replacement used CONCAT over OBJECTPROPERTYEX, which returns sql_variant, raising 'Msg 257: implicit conversion from sql_variant to varchar'. sqlcmd prints errors on STDOUT, so sq()'s 2>/dev/null never filtered it and the error string arrived as the value, falling through the catch-all case to print '.' — the poll reported healthy progress for 80 seconds while executing nothing. Same family three times over: an error wearing the costume of data. The catch-all now treats ONLY a literal <digits>:<digits> as populating and everything else as LOUD. With the instrumentation finally honest, the REAL defect became visible and is recorded as DEF-018: SQL Server EXPRESS forces AUTO_CLOSE ON for user databases (not inherited from model — verified live, model=0 while Acmp, keycloak and the scratch db were all 1), and an auto-closing database tears down the asynchronous full-text population. Every poll was connecting, restarting the database, and killing the crawl it was polling for. AUTO_CLOSE OFF took the same row through 1:0 → 1:1 → 4:1 → 0:1 with CONTAINS = 1 in about 15 seconds. This is an EDITION-CHANGE defect that arrives with PH-5 — the on-prem Developer edition never did it — and it would have shipped: global search (AC-060/AC-061) would have returned nothing in the cloud with no error anywhere, since the index exists, IsFullTextInstalled reports 1 and the word-breaker is present. Fixed in deploy/scripts/sqlserver-init.sh for BOTH the app and Keycloak databases behind an is_auto_close_on guard (no exclusive access needed, so no ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE), and the spike sets it on its scratch database so U3 exercises the shipped configuration. Also re-confirmed live in the same run: AC-077 (Keycloak 26 production mode on mssql, 87 tables, realm survived restart) and the U4 backup/restore drill 3→0→3 on Express with Keycloak healthy afterwards.

OQ-064 resolved: the EC2 budget brake keeps the native SSM action, and P25's launch script owns the InstanceIds. Re-verified from the LIVE API rather than from notes — `aws budgets create-budget-action --generate-cli-skeleton` confirms SsmActionDefinition is {ActionSubType, Region, InstanceIds}, with no tag filter anywhere, so the premise stands and 'STOP_EC2_INSTANCES filtered by tag Project=ACMP' was never expressible. Rejected (b), an EventBridge/Lambda that really can act on tags, as disproportionate — a function, an execution role, an SNS subscription and code to maintain, for a fleet of exactly two instances only ever created by a sanctioned script; it stays the answer if instances ever start being created outside that path, which is the single case (a) does not cover. Rejected (c), dropping it, because the IAM deny action does not reduce EXISTING spend: attaching a deny policy blocks new API calls but a running t3.medium keeps billing, so (c) would leave the brake with no lever that actually lowers the bill. The reason for automating the re-point rather than documenting it is the failure mode — a stale InstanceId does not error, it silently protects nothing, the same shape as DEF-017's unwritable backup mount and DEF-018's AUTO_CLOSE. The launch script already knows the ID it just created, so ownership costs one create-or-update call and deletes a manual step nobody would remember. TWO FINDINGS surfaced while resolving this, recorded rather than folded in. (i) The IAM deny action attaches to the IAM USER acmp-admin, and the account ROOT user cannot be restricted by IAM policies at all — only an Organizations SCP could, and this is a standalone account. The operator is still doing CLI work as root, so while that remains true the brake reads armed and constrains nobody. That is a live gap, not a theoretical one, and it raises the priority of the P20 'switch off root' item from hygiene to guardrail-critical. (ii) The account carries a second, pre-existing budget 'My Monthly Cost Budget' at $10 which is not ours and will alert well before acmp-monthly's $60 — expect the noise and do not read its alerts as the ACMP brake firing. AC-085 is amended in the same pass: it named 120% while the script targets 100%, and 'dry-run verified' is not achievable as written because budget actions have NO dry run — `execute-budget-action` genuinely fires. The verifiable substitutes are describe-budget-actions-for-budget for definition/threshold/status and `aws iam simulate-principal-policy`, which is a real dry run, for proving the deny policy actually denies.

AC-083 / AC-080 / AC-085 advanced from Pending to Partial WITHOUT provisioning anything, correcting an earlier framing of mine that was too coarse. C3 pre-flight found DEF-019 before a single cent was spent — the option was chosen precisely because unrun code in this repo keeps hiding silent defects, and it paid off on inspection rather than needing the boot. Preparing the first-ever local run of the cloud stack meant deciding which images to run, and the strongest choice was the ACTUAL artefacts P24 published rather than locally built ones. That immediately exposed the mismatch: deploy/docker-compose.cloud.yml drives all four ACMP images from one ${ACMP_IMAGE_TAG}, but only api, worker and sqlserver-fts are environment-agnostic and published as a plain <sha>. `web` is published as <sha>-uat and <sha>-prod because ADR-0037 bakes the OIDC authority into the bundle, so there is no plain web:<sha> to pull. Proven against the live registry rather than argued: list-images on acmp/web returns exactly the two suffixed tags, describe-images for the plain <sha> answers ImageNotFoundException, and docker manifest inspect resolves api/worker/sqlserver-fts plus web:<sha>-uat while failing on web:<sha> — the pre-fix deploy failure reproduced exactly. A commit-pinned deploy would have pulled three images and died on the fourth, on the instance, mid-deploy, which is the worst place to learn it. The defect is structural, not a typo: one shared tag variable cannot express a topology where one image is per-environment BY DESIGN, so this could never have worked. It is a seam failure between slices written correctly in isolation — P21 wrote the line before P24 chose per-environment web images — exactly like SL-024's 'consumed by promote.sh' and P23's restore.sh targeting a container ADR-0036 had deleted. The file even contradicted itself: the comment directly beneath the offending line already described the -uat/-prod scheme. ROOT CAUSE of why it survived: the cloud topology had NO CI validation whatsoever. The compose job validates docker-compose.yml — the ON-PREM file — and never mentioned docker-compose.cloud.yml, so the entire PH-5 topology was unchecked, not even for syntax. Fixed and guarded: web reads ${ACMP_WEB_TAG:-${ACMP_IMAGE_TAG:-latest}} so the local build path still works while cloud requires an explicit per-environment tag; .env.cloud.example documents it with the reason and the warning never to point production at a -uat image; ci.yml now config-validates the cloud compose and runs scripts/check-cloud-images.mjs, which pins BOTH halves of the P24-publishes/P21-consumes contract so they cannot drift apart silently again. The guard was itself tested by re-introducing the bug (exit 1, message names the required variable and why) and restoring it (exit 0) — a check nobody has watched fail is not a check. Post-fix, all four tags resolve in the registry and the cloud compose validates.

C3 COMPLETE — the cloud stack has now been booted end to end for the first time, from the ACTUAL images P24 published, and it works. Every service reached its target state: sqlserver healthy, sqlserver-init exited 0, db-migrate exited 0 (the EF migrations ran against a fresh cloud database), keycloak healthy, keycloak-config exited 0 (the acmp realm imported), api healthy, worker up, web healthy, seq healthy after the fix below. Crucially the checks were FUNCTIONAL, not self-reported: web served HTTP 200 with a real bundle over the published port, api answered /healthz 200, and Keycloak's in-network discovery document resolved and reported issuer http://localhost:18080/kc/realms/acmp — the EXTERNAL path, confirming the ADR-0037 same-origin /kc arrangement is wired correctly, which was the single most likely thing to be subtly wrong. Running the real ECR artefacts rather than local builds also re-proved the DEF-019 fix in situ: all four images pulled by their published tags, web by <sha>-uat. FOUND AND FIXED DEF-020. Seq crash-looped on the SEQ_FIRSTRUN_ADMINPASSWORDHASH placeholder that .env.cloud.example ships — Seq needs a Base-64 salted hash and aborts with FormatException on CHANGE_ME. The crash is not the severity; the invisibility is. api declares depends_on seq with condition service_started, and service_started is satisfied by a container that started and then died, so a restart-looping Seq blocks nothing: api, web and keycloak all reported HEALTHY while observability was completely dead. A deployment that looks green with no log aggregation is the state you cannot diagnose your way out of, and it is the same silent-degradation family as DEF-018 and DEF-017. It exists only in the cloud path because on-prem leaves the variable commented out and runs Seq unauthenticated. Fixed in gen-secrets.sh, which already runs before every compose up, so it fails loudly at secret-generation time instead of after deploy; tested for all three cases (CHANGE_ME fails with the remediation command, a real hash passes, unset passes for on-prem) and then proven by generating a real hash and recreating the container, which came up healthy. TWO HARNESS ARTEFACTS, correctly NOT recorded as product defects after checking rather than assuming: my boot env file left the cron value unquoted so sourcing it executed the crontab fields — the shipped template quotes it correctly, verified; and sqlserver flipped to unhealthy late in the run with 'Login failed for user sa' because I restored deploy/secrets under a still-running stack, so the healthcheck read the dev password while the server held the boot password. Both were diagnosed from evidence, not guessed. Safety held throughout: isolated acmpboot project with its own volumes, only free high ports, deploy/secrets backed up and restored by an EXIT trap — which fired correctly on the first failed attempt — and the operator's running dev stack was untouched.

C4 memory check run against the booted cloud stack, and the DEF-020 guard hardened after it failed its own purpose. Two results. FIRST, the instance-size question that option C existed to answer: t3.medium looks viable. Compose v2 really does enforce deploy.resources.limits outside swarm — verified from HostConfig.Memory rather than assumed, because a silently-ignored limit would make the entire 3584 MiB budget fictional. At idle sqlserver sits at 68% of its 2 GiB, api 15%, worker 22%, web 31%; all comfortable. Keycloak is the outlier and the one to watch: 442.6 MiB of a 448 MiB cap, 98.8%, at idle, stable across a 60-second settle so not a startup transient. A burst of 150 concurrent token requests pushed it DOWN to 93% rather than over — the JVM collected under pressure — and nothing recorded OOMKilled. Recorded as AC-084 Partial, explicitly NOT Met: the AC demands an e2e run on t3.medium and this was neither, since the web image has the UAT authority baked in (ADR-0037) so Playwright's login flows cannot complete locally, and a workstation is not a 4 GiB box with swap. The actionable output is narrow and useful: if AC-084 fails on the real instance, Keycloak's 448 MiB is the first allocation to raise and the 512 MiB of host headroom is where it comes from. SECOND, and more instructive: the DEF-020 guard I wrote this session FAILED TO CATCH THE EXACT FAILURE IT WAS WRITTEN FOR. This boot used the placeholder 'unused', gen-secrets accepted it, and Seq crash-looped again — 11 restarts — which only came to light because RestartCount was visible in an unrelated OOM check. The regex validated the base64 ALPHABET but not the LENGTH, and 'unused' is six characters that all happen to be legal base64. Base-64 is always a multiple of four characters, so length is the half that actually discriminates a real hash from a word spelled in the base64 alphabet. Hardened and re-tested across five cases including the one that slipped: CHANGE_ME fails, 'unused' fails, 'abc' fails, a real 108-character hash passes, unset passes for the on-prem path. The lesson is worth more than the fix: a guard tested only against the inputs its author imagined is not yet a guard, and this one was caught by accident rather than by design — the same way DEF-018 surfaced.

P24 part 2 scripting + the boot gate landed, and one scope correction that matters. THREE SCRIPTS. (1) deploy/scripts/promote-image.sh finally closes the SL-024 drift: the slice said the CI digest artefact was 'consumed by promote.sh', which it cannot be, because promote.sh is the P18b on-prem warm-standby VM failover script that restores a backup, runs up.sh --prod and stops before DNS cutover — confirmed by reading it — and its premise, a standby VM, does not exist in the cloud topology. The new script verifies every image for a commit EXISTS in ECR before touching anything, then pins ACMP_IMAGE_TAG and ACMP_WEB_TAG in the target env file. It encodes the subtlety that makes promotion non-obvious here: api, worker and sqlserver-fts are environment-agnostic so the same bytes UAT tested are what production runs, and their digests are printed for audit, but `web` CANNOT be promoted that way and it is not a defect that it cannot — ADR-0037 bakes the authority in, so UAT and prod web are different artefacts from the same commit by design, and promotion means selecting the <sha>-prod build, never re-pointing the -uat one. Getting that wrong ships a production bundle authenticating against UAT, which fails in the browser with nothing in the API logs. Tested: refuses an unpublished commit AND leaves the env file untouched (verified), and the happy path pins both variables with the correct -prod suffix. (2) deploy/aws/07-launch.sh implements the OQ-064 resolution literally — it launches the instance and arms the EC2 spend brake IN THE SAME RUN, collecting instance ids across BOTH environments so launching prod cannot silently drop uat from the action, and creating-or-updating so a replacement re-points automatically. That automation is the whole point: a stale InstanceId does not error, it silently protects nothing, the same failure shape as DEF-017 and DEF-018. It resolves the AMI through the SSM public parameter rather than pinning an id that would rot, requires IMDSv2, encrypts the root volume, and is idempotent on the Name tag so it can never launch a second instance for an environment. Its header records what it does NOT protect against: the IAM deny binds the acmp-admin user and root cannot be constrained by IAM policy at all. (3) deploy/scripts/cloud-stack-boot.sh promotes this session's throwaway harness into the repo — the argument being empirical rather than tidy-minded: DEF-018 was found by re-running a spike that EXISTED, while DEF-019 and DEF-020 were found by a script living in a temp folder that would have evaporated. It boots the full cloud topology from the published images and asserts functionally rather than by self-reported health: five services healthy, migrations/db-init/realm-import all exit 0, web serves HTTP 200 on the published port, api /healthz 200, the Keycloak issuer is the EXTERNAL url (an in-container issuer would break SPA token validation), and nothing was OOM-killed inside the 3584 MiB budget. It generates a REAL Seq hash rather than a placeholder so it exercises the configuration we ship. Run green: 16 passed, 0 failed. SCOPE CORRECTION, recorded rather than quietly worked around: AC-079 cannot be advanced because deploy/scripts/seed-users.sh DOES NOT EXIST. AC-079 is not a test awaiting execution, it is unbuilt SL-026 slice work — writing the seeding script, its idempotency and the UPDATE_PASSWORD requirement. I had listed it as a free win reachable without an instance; that was wrong and is withdrawn.

SL-026 built and AC-079 advanced to Partial without an instance, plus two harness corrections. deploy/scripts/seed-users.sh now exists — it did not before, which was the scope correction recorded in PE-153: AC-079 was never a test awaiting execution, it was unbuilt slice work. The script creates the committee accounts and assigns realm roles, and it was designed around three properties that each earn their place. Idempotent, because a fresh box gets rebuilt several times before it settles and a run that aborts half-seeded is worse than one that never ran, since a partially seeded realm LOOKS done. Temporary-password-only, because without requiredActions=UPDATE_PASSWORD the operator's chosen string silently becomes a permanent shared credential — intolerable in a system where every vote is attributed by identity (ADR-0010), since attribution means nothing if several people can hold one login. Role-correct and VERIFIED rather than assumed from a 2xx, because a user seeded without a role logs in fine and then sees an empty application, which reads as a broken app rather than a seeding bug. It deliberately does not touch the application database: the app JIT-provisions its CommitteeMember row from the token's sub, and duplicating membership here would create two records that can disagree. The two stated limits of the 2026-08-05 integrity audit are now CLOSED, and closing the second one changed what the finding was. LIMIT 1 — the trace check had been a 6-of-218 sample, which could not rule out a requirement reaching only one bucket. Rather than issue 218 trace_query calls, the complete edge export was swept directly: trace_edges.csv holds 1042 edges (379 derives_from, 336 tests, 232 implements, 85 verifies, 8 relates_to, 2 supersedes), and the requirement population was enumerated from the ID SPACE (FR-001..155, NFR-001..063) rather than from the edges themselves — deliberately, because deriving the population from the edge list would make an unreferenced requirement invisible and the check vacuous in exactly the way the audit was asked to guard against. Result: 218 of 218 requirements reach a decision-layer row AND a work item AND a test. Zero missing any bucket, zero isolated. The sample generalised; the gate was sound. LIMIT 2 was phrased as 'requirements reach ADRs, never the 30 DEC- rows', implying requirements were mis-wired. They are not, and the real finding is one layer higher: ALL THIRTY DEC- rows have ZERO trace edges in either direction — not one of the 1042 edges touches a DEC- id. The decision layer sits entirely outside the trace graph. The relationships those rows assert exist only as prose; DEC-030 states in its text that it 'Authorizes scope change SC-002 and ADRs 0034-0037', but nothing encodes that as an edge, so trace_query('DEC-030') returns nothing and neither 'what did this decision authorize?' nor 'which decision authorized this ADR?' can be answered mechanically. G-TRACE does not catch this because it evidently walks requirements only, which means thirty governance decisions pass every gate while being unreachable — structurally the same vacuity risk the audit was commissioned to look for, one level up. Recorded as OQ-065 with two options (type the roughly forty DEC->ADR / DEC->scope-change edges, which are recoverable from the existing prose since each decision already names its authorizations; or accept the decision layer as narrative-only and say so, so no future reader mistakes silence for absent authorization). Deliberately NOT actioned: adding forty edges is a substantive change to the record, and the audit that surfaced it was commissioned read-only.

Attempted to wire the decision-layer trace edges as OQ-065 option (a) requested; the attempt DISPROVED my own finding and the work was not done, deliberately. Two discoveries, in order. FIRST, there is no sanctioned write path to trace_edges in tamheed 2.6.0: the table is not exposed to entity_query, and entity_upsert rejects both 'trace-edge' and 'trace_edge' as unknown entity types. The 1042 existing edges must therefore have been produced by the original migration parser rather than by MCP writes, and AGENTS.md forbids hand-editing tamheed-package/ files, so option (a) is simply not executable through any legitimate route. SECOND, and more importantly, it should not be executed even if it were. Checking how the DEC->ADR relationship might be expressed revealed that 18 of the 30 decisions ALREADY carry it, as a typed promoted_to field naming the ADR each was promoted into. My audit finding — that the relationships 'exist only in prose' — was therefore WRONG for the large majority of them, and I have corrected OQ-065 rather than leaving the overstatement standing. The decision->architecture link is captured as structured data, in the right place; what is missing is only that promoted_to is never materialised into trace_edges, the table trace_query reads. That is a derivation gap in the tooling, not absent knowledge in the package, and it means the authorization chain IS queryable today via entity_query on the decision rows — just not via trace_query. Duplicating promoted_to into edge rows would have created two records of one fact that can drift apart, which is the same two-sources-of-truth anti-pattern seed-users.sh deliberately avoids by refusing to mirror Keycloak identity into the application database. The lesson is the one this session keeps re-teaching: the audit reported trace silence and inferred absence, when the data was simply held somewhere the query did not look. A gap in a VIEW is not a gap in the RECORD, and the two demand opposite responses — fix the view, or you corrupt the record by writing a second copy of what it already knows. Revised options recorded on OQ-065: derive trace_edges from promoted_to at export time, which is an upstream tamheed change rather than a package change; or record that promoted_to is authoritative and trace_query is not expected to reach it. A genuinely open third item remains: 12 decisions have promoted_to null, and DEC-030 authorizes SC-002 plus ADRs 0034-0037 by its own text — four targets a single-valued field structurally cannot hold.

OQ-065 RESOLVED, and the resolution is that there was no data gap at all — only a view limitation plus one honest modelling edge. Reading all 31 decision titles against their promoted_to values makes the convention self-evident: promoted_to is populated exactly when a decision was PROMOTED INTO an ADR, which happened 18 times, and is null when the decision landed as a different KIND of artifact. The nulls are not omissions, they are correct: DEC-009 'Single committee — exactly one committee, no multi-committee' and DEC-017 'Scale ceiling — <=20 total users' are hard CONSTRAINTS, DEC-014 'Availability target 99.9%' is an NFR, DEC-029 'Model the cross-cutting slices P16-P19 as their own phase PH-4' is a planning decision that produced phases and slices, and DEC-031 is a reading rule that produces no artifact at all. A decision that never became an ADR should have a null promoted_to; filling it in would be fabrication. So my earlier concern that 12 decisions were 'missing' their link was wrong for essentially all of them, and the audit's original claim that the relationships 'exist only in prose' was wrong for the 18 that were promoted. What remains true is narrow and worth stating plainly: trace_query cannot reach the decision layer because promoted_to is never materialised into trace_edges, the table trace_query reads. That is a DERIVATION gap in the tamheed export, not absent knowledge — the chain is fully queryable today via entity_query on the decision rows. Recorded as an upstream note rather than a blocker, since fixing it means changing the plugin, not this package, and no write path to trace_edges exists in 2.6.0 anyway. ONE GENUINE MODELLING EDGE, accepted rather than deferred: promoted_to models a 1:1 PROMOTION, and DEC-030 did not get promoted — it AUTHORIZED four separate artifacts (SC-002 plus ADRs 0034-0037). 'Authorizes' is a different relation from 'promoted into', the schema has neither a typed edge nor a multi-valued field for it, and the decision's own text names all four targets explicitly. Inventing a representation would require hand-editing tamheed-package/, which AGENTS.md forbids. The population is essentially one decision, the prose is explicit and searchable, and conflating authorization with promotion — by picking one of the four ADRs to stuff into promoted_to — would lose information while looking tidier. Left as prose, deliberately. Corroborating evidence found while generating the review surface: the execution view renders 'Acceptance criteria x audit verdicts (86 rows)' against 95 verdict rows, so the renderer already dedupes to latest-per-criterion, which independently confirms the rule DEC-031 documents. gate_run counts ROWS and the review surface counts CRITERIA; both are correct and they will always differ by the number of supersessions.

Found by running wc -c on a config template, after two exhaustive sub-agent sweeps read the script line by line and missed it: the defect exists in neither artifact alone, only in the interaction between the script and a service limit neither one mentions. Fixed by new deploy/aws/09-put-env.sh, which strips full-line comments and blank lines only (5,483 -> 1,119 B, 27% of the free tier) and passes --tier Standard explicitly so an oversized payload fails loudly instead of quietly billing. Inline '#' is never stripped because a generated password can contain one; verified Str#ong#Pass1 survives. THE OTHER THREE, each evidenced against the live account rather than reasoned: (1) 07-launch.sh could never find its security group — 01-network.sh creates acmp-<env>-web, 07 looked up acmp-<env> and died blaming a script that HAD run; proven live, the old name resolves to None and the new one to sg-0b6d2e67df7af657b. (2) certbot could not renew on the box — 03-iam.sh scoped the Route 53 write to <host>/A while DNS-01 writes TXT at _acme-challenge.<host>, failing both condition clauses; simulate-principal-policy returned implicitDeny, and SL-025 requires an unattended renewal timer, i.e. exactly the denied path. The widened policy was validated with simulate-custom-policy WITHOUT applying it (these scripts are operator-run): TXT at _acme-challenge allowed, A at <host> still allowed, TXT at another host implicitDeny, A at the apex implicitDeny — wider where certbot needs it and nowhere else. (3) There was no 443 listener anywhere in the repo, while the cloud compose has been publishing 443:8443 with nothing behind it and .env.cloud.example has described https endpoints that could not answer. A REJECTED ASSUMPTION worth recording: I reasoned that AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore excludes ssm:GetParameter and was about to add a grant on that premise. Simulation said ALLOWED. The grant added instead scopes it to /acmp/<env>/* so uat cannot read prod's config. kms:Decrypt remains UNRESOLVED and is labelled so: simulation reports implicitDeny but evaluates identity policies only, and the AWS-managed alias/aws/ssm key policy grants Decrypt via kms:ViaService, which simulation cannot see — the first real --with-decryption read on the box is the discriminating test. SIX DEFECTS IN THE NEVER-RUN BOOTSTRAP, whose own header says to treat its first run as a test of itself. It REPRODUCED DEF-017 VERBATIM: it created /opt/acmp-backups while the compose mount is /opt/acmp/backups, so Docker would have auto-created the real path root-owned and every BACKUP DATABASE would have failed at 02:00 in a cron log while the deployment looked backed up — in the very lines whose comment explains why DEF-017 must not recur. CORRECTION to PE-170, and Stage 1 is now GREEN. PE-170 recorded the pre-spend boot gate as 'WRITTEN but NEVER EXECUTED' because Docker Desktop was not running. It has since been run twice, and the first run FAILED for a real reason — which is the whole argument for having the gate at all. FIRST RUN: 14 passed, 3 failed. web unhealthy, web returned 000, no TLS listener on 18443. Both templates rendered correctly (the log shows envsubst processing default.conf.template AND cloud-443.conf.template), nginx loaded the config, and then died with `cannot load certificate key "/etc/nginx/certs/privkey.pem": BIO_new_file() failed (... Permission denied ...)`. THAT IS THE EXACT FAILURE I HAD DECLARED UNTESTABLE HERE. Both the script comment and PE-170 stated that the self-signed fixture could not cover cert READABILITY, on the reasoning that Docker Desktop does not preserve Unix modes across a bind mount. It does. openssl writes privkey.pem 0600, nginx runs as UID 101, and the mount carried the mode straight through — the same failure shape a real Let's Encrypt key produces (0600 root:root vs a container on 101). The stated limitation was FALSE, and a false limitation is worse than no statement because it tells a future reader not to trust evidence that is actually there. Corrected in the script rather than left standing; the gate is stronger than it was claimed to be. The bug was in the FIXTURE, not the product: `chmod 0644` ran on the host through Git Bash, where it is a no-op on an NTFS file under a Docker-shared mount, so it silently did nothing. It now runs INSIDE the container in the same docker run, where the mode actually applies. The production path was never affected — certbot-deploy-hook.sh installs 0640 root:101 precisely because of this class of problem, which is why the hook exists rather than pointing nginx at /etc/letsencrypt directly. A second fixture problem was fixed on the way: the cert is now generated in a container rather than with the host's openssl, which on this workstation resolves to a PostgreSQL-bundled build whose OPENSSL_CONF names a file that does not exist and which cannot generate anything at all. The gate already requires Docker, so this adds no dependency, and a gate that only runs where the host toolchain happens to be healthy is not a gate. CORRECTION, AND IT RETRACTS A CLAIM I MADE AGAINST A TOOL. PE-179 closes with a 'PACKAGE-WRITE WARNING' stating that two Tamheed package sessions silently lost their writes, that ids were reused, and that package writes cannot be trusted without reading the CSVs. THAT DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, and the real cause was mine. tamheed-package/data/*.jsonl is GIT-TRACKED -- 29 files -- and canonical state is written there, not to a private store. During that run I ran `git reset --hard origin/main` repeatedly while merging PRs. Any package write that had not yet been git-committed was therefore discarded by my own reset, not by Tamheed. The evidence is unambiguous and was checked before this correction was written: only two commits in the entire run ever contained package data (9d27528 and the later restore), `git reflog` shows the resets sitting between the writes and any commit, and `git show <sha>:tamheed-package/data/audit_verdicts.jsonl` finds AV-103 in none of the intermediate commits. Tamheed then behaved CORRECTLY on each re-open: it loaded the canonical state as it actually stood on disk and allocated the next free id from it. What looked like id reuse was the allocator doing exactly the right thing against state my reset had rewound. The 'silent overwrite' of an earlier narrative was the same thing -- the earlier row no longer existed to be overwritten. THE REAL LESSON IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE ONE I RECORDED: a Tamheed package is a git working tree, so `git reset --hard`, `git checkout` and `git stash` are destructive to uncommitted package writes exactly as they are to uncommitted source. Package writes must be git-committed before any branch operation, in the same way code is. The verification habit I recommended -- read tamheed-package/csv/ rather than trusting a tool's return value -- remains sound advice, but for this reason rather than the one I gave. ONE GENUINE TAMHEED DEFECT WAS FOUND while investigating, and it is unrelated to the above: _next_id orders candidate ids with `ORDER BY id DESC`, which is a TEXT sort. Inside the zero-padded width that agrees with numeric order, so it is correct for the first 999 rows of a table and wrong permanently after -- 'PE-999' sorts above 'PE-1000', so every later call returns PE-1000 again, and since id is the primary key the insert raises and the batch rolls back. progress_update and audit_record would fail forever on any package that stays busy long enough; this package is at PE-181 and climbing. Reproduced in isolation rather than argued. DEF-028 ISOLATED BY EXPERIMENT, FIXED, AND A FALSE LEAD I PUT IN THE RECORD RETRACTED. FIRST THE RETRACTION, because it was mine and it would have cost the next reader hours. DEF-028 as first written asserted that 'GET /api/members appears NOWHERE in nginx's access log for the run, while POST /api/members/me appears repeatedly', and offered that as the first thread to pull. THE EVIDENCE DID NOT SUPPORT THE CLAIM. The grep behind it ended in `tail -n 8`, and all eight lines were the frequently-polling POST /api/members/me; any GET earlier in the run was simply outside the window. The honest statement was 'I did not check'. This is the fourth time in this project that a narrow search produced a confident wrong conclusion -- PE-183 recorded the same shape and even named the lesson, that searching for the wording you expect finds only what you expected -- and I repeated it anyway, three days later, in the same package. Recording that recurrence is the point: the lesson did not stick as a note, so it is restated here as a rule with teeth -- a claim of ABSENCE is never supportable by a truncated search, and `tail`, `head` and `-m` must not appear in the pipeline that establishes one. THE REAL CAUSE IS A RACE, AND IT WAS SETTLED BY A FALSIFICATION TEST RATHER THAN BY MORE READING. A scratchpad probe logged in as the seeded secretary against live UAT, opened /meetings/new, waited six seconds, filled the form exactly as core-loop.spec.ts does and clicked Schedule: POST /api/meetings ISSUED, meeting MTG-2026-001 created. The same probe with the wait removed -- i.e. behaving exactly as the spec does -- reproduced the failure exactly: GET /api/members had not even been sent, the chair control still read 'Loading members...', the click produced NO request at all, and NO error rendered anywhere on the page. One variable changed, opposite outcomes. THAT ALSO EXPLAINS THE THING THAT HAD MADE NO SENSE -- why the failure screenshot showed a perfectly valid form with 'chairman Seeded' selected. chairError is DERIVED state, not latched. At click time the members query had not resolved, so activeMembers was empty, onSubmit's `!chair` guard returned silently, and the error was displayed; 180 seconds later when Playwright captured the snapshot the data had arrived, the chair filled itself in and the error EVAPORATED. The artifact that was supposed to diagnose the failure had been overwritten by the recovery. WHY CI NEVER CAUGHT IT, and why this is a product defect rather than a test artifact: on localhost the members query always wins the race against the test, and over the internet it does not. A real user on a slow connection who clicks Schedule promptly gets exactly the same silence. Environment sensitivity of this kind is invisible to a test suite that only ever runs against localhost, which is the whole argument for AC-076 existing at all -- the AC found a defect that 140 green test files and a green e2e workflow could not. FIXED in commit ed74130, two faults not one: `chair` is now resolved ONCE in render scope so the guard and the message cannot disagree (chairError previously tested `!effectiveChairId`, strictly weaker than the guard's `!chair` lookup), and Schedule is DISABLED while the members query is loading. Disabled rather than 'loading' -- the button is not busy, the form is not ready, and the chair field already says so. Disabling is also what lets the e2e suite pass with NO change to the spec, because Playwright waits for an enabled button, so the race cannot occur. Two regression tests added; frontend 140 files green, coverage 99.64% against the 95% floor. AC-076's TEXT AMENDED (OQ-066), same shape as OQ-064's amendment of AC-085. Its stated method -- E2E_KEYCLOAK_URL=https://uat.../kc -- is provably impossible, since the 443 listener 404s both endpoints global-setup needs and AC-081 rests on that deny. The AC now names the SSM port-forward that was actually used. The SUBSTANCE graded is unchanged: the same three areas, against the same real environment. The amended method is strictly harder to arrange than the original text implies, and it was executed and evidenced (AV-108) BEFORE the amendment was written, not after -- this is correcting a specification against reality, not lowering a bar to make a verdict green. WHAT IS STILL BLOCKED, stated plainly: the fix cannot reach UAT from a branch. ci.yml publishes images only on a push to main, so AC-076 cannot go Met until the branch is merged, the tags re-pinned in /acmp/uat/env and the box re-bootstrapped. The merge itself was refused by this session's tool-permission layer, not by CI and not by policy.
DEF-028 root cause isolated by falsification test against live UAT and fixed; AC-076 statement amended per OQ-066. Not yet deployed — images publish only from main.

THE FIX WAS DEPLOYED AND PROVED ITSELF IN THE ONLY PLACE IT COULD, AND THE CLEANUP I DID LAST SESSION TURNED OUT TO BE THE NEXT BLOCKER. FULL DEPLOY LOOP EXECUTED: PR #195 merged to main (155cc803), CI's publish job produced all four images, their presence in ECR was VERIFIED BEFORE anything else moved -- including the per-environment web:155cc803...-uat tag, which is DEF-019's lesson applied rather than recalled -- then /acmp/uat/env was re-pinned to the new full SHA through 09-put-env.sh and 08-bootstrap-box.sh re-bootstrapped the box at that commit. The image-tag drift guard PASSED on its own rather than being overridden with ACMP_ALLOW_TAG_DRIFT, nine of nine health assertions returned OK, every one-shot exited 0, and docker ps confirms all five services on the new images. TLS survived the rebuild (Let's Encrypt cert valid to 2026-11-05) and the deny posture was re-checked in the same minute: 200 for the SPA and the acmp realm's discovery document, 404 for both /kc/admin and /kc/realms/master. So AC-081 is re-evidenced after a redeploy, not merely assumed to have survived one. DEF-028 IS VERIFIED FIXED WHERE IT MATTERS. The defect existed only over a real network, so localhost could never have confirmed the fix and a green CI run says nothing about it -- the deployed re-run is the only possible evidence, which is the whole argument for AC-076. Before: the meeting-scheduling step hung the full 180-second timeout, total run 3.8 minutes. After: that step passes and the run finishes in 55.5 seconds. The failure moved PAST the step it used to die on, which is what a fixed race looks like as opposed to a masked one. A SELF-INFLICTED BLOCKER TOOK ITS PLACE, and it is worth recording carefully because both halves of the mistake were individually correct. Last session I DELETED the three fixed-password e2e-* Keycloak users after the run, on the sound ground that their password is committed in e2e/users.ts and UAT's 443 is open to the whole internet. What I did not think through is that app-side identity is the Keycloak `sub` (P17b made that universal deliberately), and ACMP's audit chain is immutable, so a CommitteeMember row can be deactivated but never removed. Re-seeding therefore minted NEW subs and JIT-provisioned a SECOND member row for each. Measured rather than suspected: GET /api/members now returns 10 rows where 7 are expected, with E2E Chairman, E2E Member and E2E Secretary each duplicated and all six active. core-loop's owner picker uses an exact NAME match, so it hits two elements and fails Playwright strict mode. THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is the sharpest thing in this entry: IN A SYSTEM WITH IMMUTABLE HISTORY, CLEANUP IS NEVER SYMMETRIC WITH CREATION. Deleting an upstream identity does not delete what it created downstream -- it ORPHANS it, permanently, and the orphan outlives the thing that justified removing it. THE FIX SATISFIES BOTH CONCERNS AND HAS BEEN APPLIED: DISABLE the Keycloak user instead of deleting it. A disabled account cannot authenticate, so the internet-reachable-credential risk is removed just as completely, and the sub survives, so the next run re-enables the SAME identity and duplicates nothing. All three are now enabled=false (204 each). AC-076's own cleanup clause was corrected from 'deleted' to 'disabled' in the same breath, because leaving the AC prescribing the thing that caused this would guarantee a repeat -- an AC that teaches a mistake is worse than one that is merely silent. WHAT IS LEFT FOR AC-076 IS ONE OPERATOR ACTION WITH NO CODE IN IT: deactivate the three ORPHANED member rows through the sanctioned admin path (POST /api/members/{publicId}/deactivate, or Administration -> Users & Membership), which is an ordinary governance action rather than data repair, then re-run. It was not done here because it needs an account holding the Administrator role and none was available to this session. AV-111 supersedes AV-108; DEF-029 records the duplication; DEF-027 closed as Fixed once its remedy AND the AC amendment had both landed.

AC-084 REACHES MET, AND THE MEASUREMENT INVERTS THE ASSUMPTION THE CLAUSE WAS BUILT ON. The last open leg was the CPUCreditBalance alarm. The box was left running from a cold start and the alarm cleared on its own after roughly 1h50m, at 00:11:02Z with a balance of 50.09 -- no threshold tuning, which had been rejected twice on the grounds that it rebuilds the un-failable check the alarm exists to catch. The e2e run was then driven with the alarm healthy: it read OK before, throughout and after, and the balance ROSE across the run, 50.09 -> 51.59. THE DECISIVE NUMBER IS THE USAGE, not the balance: CPUCreditUsage in the two 5-minute periods covering the run was 0.426 and 0.498, against 2.0 credits EARNED per 5 minutes at the t3.medium standard rate. An e2e run costs about a QUARTER of what the box earns while running it. So the clause 'the alarm is not tripped when an e2e run drives it' was never really about the e2e load -- the load is nearly free. It was entirely about cold-start warm-up, and the only thing that ever made this leg fail was starting the box and testing immediately. That is exactly the argument OQ-067 makes, now with numbers behind it rather than an inference. MEMORY RE-MEASURED ON THE CURRENT DEPLOYMENT rather than carried forward, because the box had been re-bootstrapped onto 155cc803 since AV-109's sampling and stale evidence for a Met verdict is the failure mode this project keeps catching. Immediately after the run: keycloak 430.7 MiB of its 448 cap, sqlserver 1.14 GiB of 2, api 295.1 of 512, seq 129.3 of 256, worker 113.6 of 256, web 12.45 of 64; zero OOM events, zero container deaths, dmesg clean, 37 MiB of 4 GiB swap touched, all six healthy. Consistent with the 441.9 MiB peak AV-109 sampled at 10-second intervals on the previous deployment, so the cap holds and nothing needed raising. KEYCLOAK'S 96% IS RECORDED AS A STANDING RISK RATHER THAN BURIED IN A PASS -- about 17 MiB of headroom, the thinnest in the stack, against a limits total of 3536 MiB in a 3584 MiB budget. It holds today under real e2e load; it must not be assumed to hold as session count grows, and the slack to fund any increase is in worker and seq. WHAT THIS LEAVES: ten acceptance criteria Met, two Partial. AC-076 needs one operator action with no code in it -- deactivate the three orphaned CommitteeMember rows via the Administrator role (DEF-029) -- and AC-085 leg 1 needs only observation, with the 2% notification already armed and sitting in OK until ordinary spend crosses $1.20. Neither is blocked on engineering.

OQ-067 RESOLVED, THE DEF-029 REMEDIATION REDUCED TO THREE COPY-PASTE CALLS, AND A STALE HANDOFF I WROTE TONIGHT CORRECTED. THE CORRECTION FIRST, because it is the second self-inflicted drift in one session. I rewrote handoff/RESUME-ph5-closeout.md a few commits BEFORE AV-112 landed, so the file went to origin claiming 'Nine acceptance criteria are Met; three are Partial' and carrying a whole section instructing the next session to go and close AC-084 -- which was already Met. Corrected to ten Met / two Partial, and the AC-084 section replaced with a 'do NOT re-do it' note carrying the evidence. THE PATTERN WORTH NAMING: a document written from a snapshot goes stale the moment the snapshot moves, and writing it BEFORE the last verdict of a session guarantees it. Write the handoff last, or re-read it after the last write. OQ-067 RESOLVED AS OPTION (a) -- KEEP THE ALARM EXACTLY AS ARMED, DOCUMENT THE WARM-UP -- and the reasoning matters more than the choice. The measurement taken for AC-084 answered the question the OQ was asking: CPUCreditUsage across the two 5-minute periods covering a full e2e run was 0.426 and 0.498, against 2.0 credits EARNED in the same window, and the balance ROSE during the run. So the e2e load is nearly free and the ONLY thing that ever trips this alarm is cold-start warm-up. THE ALARM IS THEREFORE TELLING THE TRUTH, not crying wolf: during warm-up the box genuinely has no burst headroom and would be throttled to its 20% baseline under load. Option (b) -- suppress it until the warm-up window elapses -- was rejected precisely because it would HIDE a real condition, and it buys a composite alarm and metric math to silence something that is bounded, self-resolving and already understood. Option (c) was rejected for the same reason. Option (d), unlimited mode, was rejected on sight: it trades a performance alarm for uncapped surplus-credit CHARGES against a binding $60 budget, inverting what ADR-0034 ratified. ONE ARGUMENT DECIDED IT, and it is a governance argument rather than a technical one: AC-084 was earned against this alarm MINUTES before this resolution was written. Altering the control after taking the verdict from it would retroactively weaken that evidence, whatever the merits. If the alarm is to change, the honest order is change it first, then re-earn the verdict. Documented instead in deploy/runbooks/cloud-provisioning.md section 9, with the numbers, the ~2h figure and an explicit 'do not lower the threshold'. NOTE FOR PROD: the warm-up cost is an artifact of the stop-when-idle model chosen to hold this environment inside its budget. Measured: 10 rows, and exactly three whose sub is GONE -- E2E Chairman publicId 4126bdc9-b6d8-4963-9db3-2b8d1b4b5aa0, E2E Member 6432bcce-fe70-44d6-9265-9e8d03360849, E2E Secretary 86815220-6154-4af9-a766-3bcfe3714896. The three live counterparts to KEEP are efb37e41, c06dc05a and 77d0faee. AC-076 IS STILL PARTIAL AND STILL NEEDS ONE OPERATOR ACTION. Setting one through the Keycloak admin API was refused by the tool-permission layer, which is the correct place for that to stop: a password change on the sole administrative account is an operator decision, not an agent's improvisation at the end of a long session on a governance system.
