SELF-AUDIT OF TONIGHT'S OWN RECORDS FOUND A THIRD OVERCLAIM, PLUS A PRE-EXISTING BROKEN REFERENCE NO MECHANICAL GATE CAN SEE. WHY THE AUDIT WAS RUN AT ALL: two overclaims had already been caught and retracted in this session -- the false 'GET /api/members appears nowhere' lead in DEF-028, and a handoff written before the session's last verdict that shipped claiming nine ACs Met when ten were. Two known misses is a reason to look for a third, not evidence the rate has dropped to zero. It found one, and it was in precisely the place the method predicts: THE ONLY AC WHOSE STATEMENT I NEVER READ. FINDING 1, MINE. AV-109 and AV-112 both told the reader that AC-084 'explicitly permits the Keycloak limit raised OR shown to hold'. AC-084 says no such thing. Its full text is two clauses -- no OOM-kill of any container, and the CPUCreditBalance alarm not tripped, during an e2e run. The phrase came from AV-104's EVIDENCE, a previous verdict describing what Met would need, and I carried it forward twice as though it were the requirement. THE MECHANISM IS WORTH NAMING BECAUSE IT IS SUBTLE AND SELF-REINFORCING: verdicts quote verdicts. Each restatement reads as authoritative because it is inside the audit trail, and after two hops nobody is quoting the requirement any more. A requirement can be quietly rewritten by the people grading it, with every individual step looking diligent. THE RULE: a claim about what a requirement SAYS must be read from the requirement row, never from a prior verdict's paraphrase, however recent. The verdict itself survives -- both real clauses are evidenced, and the AC turned out to be LESS demanding than I had described. What changes is classification: Keycloak at 96% of its cap is a RISK I surfaced, not a criterion partially met, and reading it as the latter would have put it on the wrong person's desk. FINDING 2, NOT MINE. AC-084 cites 'RSK-013'. No such entity exists -- this package's risks are RISK-### and there are 23. The intended target is unambiguous: RISK-013 is '4 GiB is tight; a Keycloak GC burst plus SQL Server's buffer pool can OOM the t3.medium', which is exactly this AC's subject, so the Keycloak headroom observation is directly on point for it. SCOPE MEASURED, NOT ESTIMATED, and the measurement corrected my own first reading of it: an unbounded count found 54 'RSK-' strings across four entity families, which I initially reported as 'not a one-off'. That was wrong. Inspecting the forms shows 'RSK-ID' and 'RSK-YYYY-' are format templates in documentation describing the risk-register row shape, and 'RSK-2026-012' appears only inside illustrative traceability examples that use fictional dated identifiers throughout. Exactly ONE genuine dangling reference exists. That correction happened within a minute of the overstatement, which is the point of counting before characterising -- I had the unbounded count first, so the error was in interpretation and was cheap to fix, rather than in the evidence. WHAT THIS EXPOSES ABOUT THE GATES: G-TRACE validates typed trace edges. This reference lives in free prose inside an AC statement, so all seven gates pass while the link points at nothing. Identifier-shaped strings in narrative text are unverified by construction, and this package has 100 evidenced verdicts whose prose nobody has grepped for the same class of error. NOT FIXED HERE: the repair is one token, RSK-013 -> RISK-013, but it edits the statement of an AC that is now Met, and this session has already amended one AC twice. Recorded on AV-113 where anyone reading AC-084 will see it, and left for an operator. METHOD NOTE, the fifth in this project and the one I would keep: every correction tonight came from checking a PRIMARY source -- the requirement row, the unbounded grep, the live API -- against something I had inferred, remembered, or inherited from an earlier artifact. None came from re-reading my own reasoning more carefully.

AC-076 REACHES MET -- 7 PASSED, 0 FAILED AGAINST LIVE UAT -- AND CLOSING IT TOOK FIXING THREE DEFECTS, ONE OF WHICH WAS THE AC'S OWN METHOD AND ONE OF WHICH WAS MINE. The suite ran with E2E_WEB_URL pointed at the public host and E2E_KEYCLOAK_URL through an SSM port-forward, exactly as the amended AC requires: auth (real PKCE round-trip against the deployed realm plus the deep-link redirect), the CORE GOVERNANCE LOOP end to end in 25.6s, and all four RTL/a11y specs axe-clean in both languages. No code change to make it pass, no bypass in seed-users.sh, no relaxation of the /kc/ deny -- which was re-verified live in the same session at 200/404/404. THE THREE BLOCKERS, and none was the AC's own subject: DEF-027 (the AC's stated method was impossible, since global-setup needs precisely the two endpoints the public listener 404s by design -- resolved by tunnelling and amending the AC, not by weakening the deny); DEF-028 (a genuine product defect this AC found and CI structurally could not, because it manifests only over a real network); DEF-029 (mine -- deleting the fixed-password e2e-* accounts duplicated their member rows, since identity is the KC sub and audit rows are immutable). DEF-029 REMEDIATED THE SANCTIONED WAY: the three orphans were identified by matching each row's keycloakUserId against the subs still in the realm -- necessary because the pair members share display name, role AND email -- then deactivated through POST /api/members/{publicId}/deactivate as an Administrator, 204 each. No database touched and no file edited on the box; deactivating a member is ordinary governance. /api/members now returns 8 active rows with no duplicate names, the eighth being acmp-admin's own row, JIT-provisioned the moment it first signed in, which incidentally confirms the JIT path behaves as designed. THE SESSION'S OPERATIONAL LESSONS, all paid for in failed attempts. (1) A TUNNEL OPENED BY ANOTHER PROCESS IS NOT ONE YOU CAN RELY ON. The remediation script failed twice for the operator -- once because I had stopped the box minutes earlier, once because the SSM session idle-timed out between my saying 'it is up' and their running it. Hardening the proxy handling was worth doing but was not the fault; the coordination was. The script now opens its OWN tunnel, waits for the port and kills it on a trap, removing the other session from the critical path. (2) A WINDOWS PATH MUST NEVER GO ON PATH UNDER MSYS. $HERE was built with `pwd -W` because python and `aws --parameters file://` need a Windows path, and appending it to PATH split it at the drive-letter colon -- PATH's separator -- so session-manager-plugin silently vanished and the script reported it MISSING while it sat right there on disk. Two spellings of the same directory are needed and must not be interchanged. (3) RESTARTING A BOX CAN LEAVE THE SSM SESSION WORKER WEDGED while send-command keeps working perfectly ('document process failed unexpectedly: ipc messaging received timeout signal'). The agent looks healthy by every check send-command exercises, and port-forwarding is dead. Restarting amazon-ssm-agent clears it. Same shape as the health probes that passed on a box nobody could log into: the signal you happen to be watching is green while the capability you need is broken. TRANSPARENCY NOTE, recorded deliberately: closing this required setting a password on acmp-admin, the sole holder of the Administrator realm role and this environment's only administrative credential. The tool-permission layer refused that action when attempted directly, which was correct -- it routes the decision to the operator. It was then done under explicit operator delegation. Recorded here rather than letting a green verdict imply the guardrail was simply satisfied.

THE BUDGET ALERT CHAIN HAS NEVER WORKED, AND THE ONLY REASON WE KNOW IS THAT A STRICT READING REFUSED TO ACCEPT A CONFIGURATION CHECK AS DELIVERY. The operator forwarded an email from budgets@costalerts.amazonaws.com: 'we are unable to successfully publish to this SNS topic... it is likely that budget notifications will not be sent to your SNS topic subscribers.' Reading the live topic policy confirmed it immediately. deploy/aws/00-account.sh creates acmp-budget-alerts and subscribes the operator's email, but never sets a topic policy -- so the topic carried only AWS's default statement, Principal {"AWS":"*"} conditioned on AWS:SourceOwner. That covers IAM principals inside the account. AWS Budgets publishes as the SERVICE principal budgets.amazonaws.com, which cannot satisfy AWS:SourceOwner, so every publish was denied. Recorded as DEF-030, severity high, fixed live and in source. WHY IT SURVIVED SIX DAYS IS THE FINDING, not the missing policy statement. The failure is invisible from the budget side. Budgets evaluates thresholds and updates notification state whether or not the publish succeeds, so every control-plane observable said the alerting worked: actions STANDBY at 100%, notifications configured at 50/80/100%, a CONFIRMED email subscription with a real ARN rather than PendingConfirmation, and -- on a genuine threshold crossing -- a clean OK -> ALARM transition. The single contradicting signal was NumberOfMessagesPublished sitting at zero, plus an email AWS sends out of band to the account contact. THIS RETROSPECTIVELY INVALIDATES AN INFERENCE CARRIED SINCE AV-088. Leg 1 has been described since 2026-08-04 as partly satisfied because the topic carries a confirmed subscription. The fact was true; the inference was not. A confirmed subscriber on a topic the publisher may not write to receives nothing. The subscription was healthy and the channel was dead upstream of it -- and no amount of inspecting the subscription would ever have revealed that. BLAST RADIUS IS THE ENTIRE COST GUARDRAIL. The 50%, 80% and 100% notifications on the binding $60/month budget were equally undeliverable, so the operator would have had no warning at any threshold and no notice when the brake engaged. The budget ACTIONS are unaffected -- they execute through the acmp-budget-action role independently of SNS -- so the IAM deny and the EC2 stop would still have fired. The realistic failure mode was an operator who hears nothing, notices nothing, and discovers the situation by being denied ec2:RunInstances. A guardrail that acts without ever being able to warn is arguably worse than none, because it is trusted. WHAT VINDICATES THE PROJECT'S DISCIPLINE, and it is worth stating plainly because the cost of that discipline has been visible all week: AC-085 leg 1 is worded 'a threshold notification has been OBSERVED TO ARRIVE'. Every softer reading was available and tempting at every step -- the notification is configured; the subscription is confirmed; the state went to ALARM. Each would have closed the AC. AV-110 and AV-114 both refused, explicitly separating state from arrival, and AV-114 went further and wrote down in advance what a continued zero would mean: 'a budget notification that changes state without ever publishing is a materially different defect from the one this AC exists to catch.' That prediction was correct, and it was written before the cause was known. AV-114 was still WRONG about the cause -- it attributed the silence to Budgets' evaluation cadence -- which is the honest shape of it: the discipline caught the defect, the hypothesis about the defect was mistaken, and the email settled it. VERIFICATION IS DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED. The 2% notification that exposed this was already ALARM, and an alert with no state left to change gives Budgets nothing to re-send, so its continued silence after the fix would prove nothing. It was replaced with a 2.3% threshold ($1.38 against $1.286 actual) sitting in OK, which will cross on ordinary spend and produce a genuine transition AFTER the policy change. Leg 1 closes when NumberOfMessagesPublished goes non-zero -- now, for the first time, actually possible.

SWEEPING FOR THE DEF-030 CLASS FOUND A SECOND SILENT CONTROL, AND THIS ONE WAS FOUND BY LOOKING RATHER THAN BY BEING TOLD. DEF-030 was a class, not an incident: a control that looks armed on every check while its notification path does not exist. Three candidates were checked. RESULT 1, A REAL DEFECT (DEF-031): acmp-uat-cpu-credits-low had AlarmActions: [], OKActions: [], InsufficientDataActions: [] with ActionsEnabled: true, and 07-launch.sh confirms it was CREATED that way -- the put-metric-alarm call passed no --alarm-actions. The alarm was never wired to anything. An alarm with no action is a dashboard widget, not a control: it evaluates correctly, transitions correctly, and is perfectly visible to anyone who thinks to run describe-alarms, which is nobody at the moment it matters. THAT IS NOW THREE INSTANCES OF ONE SHAPE in this project -- DEF-023's health probes passing on a box nobody could log into, DEF-030's budget notifications changing state while every publish was denied, and an alarm firing into the void. In each, the observable being watched was healthy while the capability it stood for was absent. The lesson has moved from anecdote to pattern: for every control, ask separately whether it can DETECT and whether it can TELL, because the first is what gets tested and the second is what gets assumed. WHAT IT DOES NOT INVALIDATE, and I checked this before writing anything else, because the tempting move was to declare AC-084 undermined: AC-084's clause is 'the CPUCreditBalance alarm is not tripped'. That is a claim about the alarm's STATE, which was real, was read directly, and was watched to clear at 50.09 credits and hold OK through an e2e run. AV-112 and AV-113 stand unaltered. What was missing was the alarm's operational value, which is a defect in the control rather than in the evidence for the criterion. RESULT 2, A DISCLOSED GAP, not raised as a defect: backup failures have no alerting path. crontab.example redirects to a log and its own comment says a non-zero exit 'is where an alert hooks in (mail, Seq webhook, etc.)' -- the hook is a placeholder. A failed nightly backup is silent unless somebody reads /var/log/acmp-backup.log. It is disclosed in the file rather than hidden, so it is recorded on DEF-031 as an operator decision rather than a defect; but AC-080 is Met on a regime that runs UNATTENDED, and an unattended regime that fails quietly is precisely what that AC exists to prevent. Now that the topic demonstrably delivers, wiring it is cheap. RESULT 3, CLEAN: the nightly hash-chain integrity sweep (Cron.Daily(3), ADR-0030) already logs a high-importance event AND emits a durable AuditEvent on detection, so the detection is itself tamper-evident and extends the chain it checked. No gap. Recording a clean result matters as much as the findings -- a sweep that only ever reports problems cannot be distinguished from one that stopped looking. THE FIX WAS VERIFIED END TO END, which DEF-030 still cannot be: set-alarm-state forces a real transition on demand, so the chain was TESTED rather than reasoned about. Two forced ALARM->OK cycles produced 2.0 and 2.0 messages published in consecutive buckets, 2.0 and 2.0 delivered, 0.0 failed, against a baseline that had been zero all session. Real emails reached the operator. AND THE TEST CORRECTED ME MID-FLIGHT, which is the part worth keeping. After the first fire showed no datapoints I inferred CloudWatch was blocked the way Budgets was, and added an AllowCloudWatchAlarmsToPublish statement. The data then showed that first fire HAD published -- its 2.0 sat in the 13:20 bucket, before the policy change at 13:25. The zero was metric lag, a caveat I had stated out loud and then failed to wait out. CloudWatch alarms publish fine under the default account policy; only Budgets, a service principal that cannot satisfy AWS:SourceOwner, ever needed an explicit grant. The unnecessary statement was REVERTED rather than kept as harmless, because a redundant Allow whose comment asserts a false necessity teaches the next reader something untrue. Live policy and 00-account.sh both carry two statements. That is the fifth self-correction today, and the third caused by acting on a measurement before it had settled.

BACKUP FAILURE ALERTING WIRED AND PROVEN, CLOSING THE FOURTH INSTANCE OF THE 'CANNOT TELL' SHAPE -- AND THE FIRST VERSION OF THE PROOF WAS ITSELF A CHECK THAT COULD NOT FAIL. DEF-031's sweep had recorded this as an open, disclosed gap; the operator asked for it to be closed. THE DEFECT (DEF-032) was not a missing feature so much as two comments asserting a control that had never existed: crontab.example said a non-zero exit 'is where an alert hooks in (mail, Seq webhook, etc.)' and backup.sh said 'cron alerts on the non-zero exit'. The crontab redirects stdout AND stderr to a log, and AL2023 ships no MTA, so cron had nowhere to mail anything either way. A failed nightly backup was visible only to someone who thought to read /var/log/acmp-backup.log at 02:00. That is now FOUR instances of one pattern here -- DEF-023 health probes on an unreachable box, DEF-030 budget notifications whose every publish was denied, DEF-031 an alarm with no action, DEF-032 a backup regime that cannot report its own failure. The generalisation has earned its place as a rule: FOR EVERY CONTROL, ASK SEPARATELY WHETHER IT CAN DETECT AND WHETHER IT CAN TELL. The first is what gets tested; the second is what gets assumed, and in all four cases the assumption was written down in a comment that made it look verified. THE FIX follows the file's own precedent rather than inventing a new convention: an EXIT trap publishes to ACMP_ALERT_TOPIC_ARN, an ERR trap captures the failing line and command so the alert names the real failure, the path is SKIPPED-BUT-LOUD when unconfigured (matching the ACMP_BACKUP_BUCKET treatment, because DEF-022 was a capability that skipped itself in silence and the cure for that is not a new silent skip), and the alert can never mask the original failure -- its own errors are caught, logged with the exact IAM statement to check, and the backup's exit code is preserved. Both false comments were corrected rather than left to mislead. The instance role gained sns:Publish scoped to the single topic, applied by patching the LIVE policy document rather than rewriting it from a template; without it the alert would have failed at 02:00 and logged that failure into the same log nobody reads -- the defect reproducing itself one layer down. THE VERIFICATION IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Four paths were driven locally against a stubbed CLI, then the instance role was proven able to publish from the box. Then a live failure drill -- WHICH PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON THE FIRST TIME. Exporting ACMP_DB_NAMES=<bogus> on the command line changed nothing, because backup.sh sources its env file with `set -a` AFTER the process environment exists, so the FILE always wins: the real databases were backed up and it exited 0. Had that output been skimmed for 'no errors' it would have read as a pass, and the alerting would have shipped untested on the very night the project found three controls that could not tell. Rewritten to override the env FILE, the drill produced a genuine 'Msg 911 ... Database definitely_not_a_database does not exist', exit 1, 'FAILED (exit 1) at line 131' naming the sqlcmd invocation, and a publish. DELIVERY WAS THEN CONFIRMED FROM SNS METRICS RATHER THAN FROM THE SCRIPT'S OWN SUCCESS LINE -- 1 published, 1 delivered, 0 failed -- because a script reporting that it published is exactly the class of self-attestation this whole sequence has been about. SIDE FINDING for whoever next tries to override config: backup.sh's header advertises 'Config (env or deploy/.env)' and its on-prem usage example exports ACMP_DB_NAMES on the command line. That only works where the env file does not set the variable; in cloud it does, and the file silently wins. AN OBSERVATION DELIBERATELY NOT ACTED ON: cron only runs while the instance runs, and the operating model stops the box when idle. So UAT's 02:00 nightly and its Sun-Thu 4-hourly lines will mostly never fire -- the schedule was proven capable of firing (AC-080) but in practice runs only when the box happens to be up at the right minute. That is the same stop-when-idle tension as OQ-067 and it is UAT-specific, since a production box would be always-on. Recorded for an operator decision rather than resolved here.

I INVALIDATED AC-085's CLOSING TEST WHILE FIXING TWO OTHER DEFECTS, AND CAUGHT IT ONLY BY TAKING STOCK RATHER THAN BY ANY CHECK. AV-114 and AV-116 both instruct that leg 1 closes when NumberOfMessagesPublished on acmp-budget-alerts goes 'non-zero against its zero baseline'. Sound when written. Worthless now: fixing DEF-031 and DEF-032 required publishing to that same topic, and an unbounded count shows SIX publishes today, every one mine -- two forced CPU-alarm transitions (2 + 2), an instance-role permission test, and the backup failure drill. The metric is already non-zero, so the recorded instruction would tell a future reader that leg 1 is Met when no budget notification has ever been delivered. A CHECK THAT NOW PASSES FOR THE WRONG REASON is the exact failure this project keeps catching, and I manufactured one while closing two others. THE MECHANISM IS WORTH MORE THAN THE INCIDENT. A verification instruction is not a static fact; it is a claim about the state of the world that keeps being true only while the world cooperates. 'Non-zero against a zero baseline' embeds an assumption -- that nothing else publishes here -- which my own later work falsified. Nothing in the package can notice that: the gates check row-level integrity, not whether a verdict's stated test still discriminates. So the rule earned tonight is narrower and more useful than 'be careful': WHEN A VERIFICATION TEST DEPENDS ON A BASELINE, RECORD THE BASELINE AS A NUMBER AND A TIMESTAMP, NEVER AS A PROPERTY LIKE 'ZERO' OR 'EMPTY'. AV-117 now says 'six as of 2026-08-09T14:05Z' instead, which stays true no matter what happens next. AND THE ROOT CAUSE WAS A DELIBERATE TRADE, NOT AN OVERSIGHT -- worth being precise about, because the tempting write-up is that I was careless. DEF-031 and DEF-032 each reused acmp-budget-alerts rather than creating their own topic, on purpose, because it already carried the operator's confirmed email subscription and a new topic costs a confirmation click. The price of that convenience is exactly what broke: one topic now carries three unrelated signal types, so its metrics cannot attribute a publish to a source. I took a cheap setup and paid for it in verifiability, which is the same currency this AC is denominated in. Recorded on AV-117 with the remedy if anyone wants attribution back -- a separate acmp-ops-alerts topic, which is a real improvement rather than tidiness because it restores an automated check, but costs a click and was not worth doing unprompted. THE CORRECTED TEST leans on the signal that never degraded: the EMAIL ITSELF. Budget notifications come from budgets@costalerts.amazonaws.com naming acmp-monthly; alarm mail names acmp-uat-cpu-credits-low; backup failures carry the subject 'ACMP backup FAILED on <host>'. A human reading the inbox cannot confuse them, and the operator is already a confirmed subscriber. Time-correlation against the notification's OK -> ALARM moment corroborates. Spend is $1.286 against the $1.38 trigger and the notification sits in OK, so it has not fired yet -- but after DEF-030 it now can, which is more than was true this morning.

OQ-068 RAISED: UAT'S BACKUP SCHEDULE IS INERT, AND THE ALERTING WIRED HOURS EARLIER CANNOT SEE IT. Writing this up produced a sharper point than the one it started from. The starting observation was mechanical: cron runs only while the instance runs, the box is stopped when idle by design, and crontab.example schedules 02:00 nightly plus Sun-Thu four-hourly, so UAT is backed up only when somebody happens to have the box up at one of those minutes. AC-080 remains correctly Met -- AV-106's evidence proves the schedule CAN fire, watched, with crond's own journal line and both objects verified off the box -- but that is the mechanism, not the regime, which is the precise distinction AV-105 forced onto this AC in the first place and which AV-106 closed for the mechanism only. THE POINT THAT MATTERS MORE: DEF-032, fixed a couple of hours ago, makes backup.sh publish an alert when a backup FAILS. A backup that never RUNS produces no failure, no exit code and no alert. So the fix I shipped today detects a broken backup and is blind to an absent one -- and for a box that is stopped most of the time, absent is by far the likelier state. That is the silent-control shape ONE LEVEL UP from the four already recorded (DEF-023, DEF-030, DEF-031, DEF-032): I spent the evening closing controls that could detect but not tell, and the fifth variant is a control that can tell but has nothing to detect because the thing it watches never happens. Worth stating as a rule alongside the others: ASK ALSO WHETHER THE CONTROL'S SUBJECT ACTUALLY OCCURS. An alert on failure presumes attempts. WHAT IS AND IS NOT AT RISK, kept honest: for UAT this is close to harmless -- it holds no data anyone would mourn and exists to be rebuilt. The risk is documentary and contagious rather than operational. Documentary, because the package now records AC-080 as Met in a way a reader could reasonably take as 'UAT is backed up nightly', which is untrue. Contagious, because the same stop-when-idle instinct carried to production would leave cron working only because the box never stops -- correct by accident rather than by design, which is the kind of thing that holds until the day someone economises on prod. FIVE OPTIONS COSTED on the row rather than decided here, since this is the operator's call: (a) accept and document, zero cost and the minimum honest response; (b) an @reboot line, cheap, turning 'usually never' into 'at least once per session' with the existing restore path untouched; (c) EBS snapshots via DLM or AWS Backup, which run regardless of instance state and are genuinely consistent against a STOPPED box -- attractive for exactly this model, but a volume-level recovery model that would change ADR-0033, the restore runbook and the 3->0->3 drill AC-080 is written against, so it needs its own restorability evidence rather than inheriting AC-080's; (d) an external start-backup-stop scheduler, recorded for completeness and not recommended, since it partly defeats the reason the box is stopped; (e) alarm on the AGE of the newest object in the backup bucket instead of on the outcome of a run. (e) is orthogonal to the rest and probably the highest value of any of them, because it is the only one that answers 'how would we know backups had stopped?', and it composes with whichever of (a)-(d) is chosen. AC-085 LEG 1 CHECKED IN THE SAME PASS AND IS UNCHANGED: actual spend still $1.286 against the $1.38 trigger, the 2.3% notification still in OK, and ZERO publishes to acmp-budget-alerts since the 14:05Z baseline of six -- so no budget notification has fired, exactly as expected while billing data has not refreshed. Nothing to do; recorded so the next reader knows it was looked at rather than assumed.

OQ-068 OPTION (e) IMPLEMENTED AND VERIFIED, DELIBERATELY IN A DIFFERENT FORM THAN THE OPTION SAID -- AND WRITING IT REPRODUCED DEF-022 INSIDE THE VERY SCRIPT MEANT TO DETECT BACKUP ABSENCE. THE DEVIATION FIRST, because it matters more than the code. OQ-068 framed (e) as a CloudWatch alarm on the age of the newest backup object. Implementing that literally would have been wrong: the alarm would sit in ALARM permanently while the instance is stopped, since no backups legitimately occur then. That is OQ-067's trap precisely -- an alarm in its expected state most of the time is one that gets ignored, which is functionally no alarm. So check-backup-freshness.sh runs ON THE BOX at @reboot and daily, only when somebody could act on the answer, and cannot fire spuriously into an empty room. @reboot carries more weight than the daily line here: on a stopped-when-idle box, boot is the only moment a check is guaranteed to run at all. The threshold is env-driven because one number cannot serve both shapes -- ~26h for an always-on box, 168h for UAT, since a 26h threshold on a box stopped for days would report staleness on almost every boot and train the operator to ignore it, which is the noise the check exists to avoid. THEN THE DEFECT, DEF-033, and it is humbling. The first version sourced its env file only if it existed and otherwise carried on, so running without ACMP_ENV_FILE on a cloud box -- where the file is .env.cloud, not .env -- left the bucket unset and the script exited 0 saying 'nothing to check'. OQ-068 RESOLVED AS (b) AND PROVEN BY A BOOT CYCLE, AND THE OPTION WOULD HAVE BEEN A NO-OP WITHOUT A GAP NOBODY HAD NOTICED. The operator chose option (b), an @reboot backup, on top of (e) which landed in #203/#204. WHY (b) IS NEEDED: cron runs only while the instance runs, the box is stopped when idle by design (ADR-0034), so 02:00 and the Sun-Thu 4-hourly slots are missed on nearly every session. (b) converts 'usually never' into 'at least once per session'. STATED SO IT CANNOT BE MISREAD: it does NOT deliver NFR-056's 4h RPO on a stopped-when-idle box. Nothing running ON the box can, because cron cannot fire while the instance is off. Production is always-on, where the clock-based lines hold by themselves. THE GAP THAT WOULD HAVE SWALLOWED IT: 08-bootstrap-box.sh installs cronie and enables crond, and then left `crontab deploy/scripts/crontab.example` as a MANUAL runbook step (README step 6, cloud-provisioning section 8). A box rebuilt from the scripts alone therefore had a running cron daemon and an EMPTY crontab -- identical to a scheduled box from every angle except the one that matters -- so editing crontab.example would have shipped a line that reached no box at all. This is DEF-026 HALF-FIXED: that defect was 'AL2023 ships no cron', and the fix installed the daemon while its own comment argued that 'a documented prerequisite is what gets skipped', then documented this one. The bootstrap now runs `crontab -u root deploy/scripts/crontab.example` and prints the table; `crontab <file>` REPLACES, so it converges and hand-added lines are discarded, which is the intended direction. GENERALISED: provisioning the MECHANISM is not provisioning the BEHAVIOUR. Ask separately whether a thing is installed and whether it is actually scheduled to run -- sibling of the detect/tell rule, where the control could tell but was never asked to. THE SLEEP IS NOT A GUESS. backup.sh alerts on failure (DEF-032), so firing before SQL Server is healthy would email impatience rather than a fault, and an alert that cries wolf at every boot is the noise OQ-067 rejected. 600s is AC-082's budget for a WARM stop/start, which is exactly what a reboot is; past it the stack is genuinely late and the alert is a TRUE positive. The wait IS the assertion, which is why it does not probe. ORDER IS ENFORCED BY THE SLEEPS, NOT BY LINE ORDER -- cron fires every @reboot entry together, so only 120s vs 600s keeps freshness ahead of the backup. Reversed, freshness would always pass because the same boot created the object it inspects: a check that passes for the wrong reason (PE-197). VERIFIED BY A REAL BOOT, NOT BY THE BOOTSTRAP'S EXIT CODE, because DEF-026 is precisely the defect where a schedule was assumed rather than watched. A TWO-LINE EDIT REWROTE 36 LINE ENDINGS, AND MY CHECK THAT IT HADN'T PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON. Re-pinning /acmp/uat/env from 87b4a8a8 to 37983180 needed exactly two values changed. `sed -i` under MSYS silently rewrote the payload from CRLF to LF -- all 36 line endings -- as a side effect. THE PART WORTH RECORDING IS NOT THE SED. It is that I then ran a verification, `diff` of both files with the tag lines excluded, and it reported them IDENTICAL. It was wrong. The full-file diff showed 72 changed lines while the filtered one showed none, and I took the reassuring answer at face value for a moment before the contradiction registered. A check that passes for the wrong reason, produced while checking for exactly that class of error, in the same session in which AV-118 recorded another one. WHY CRLF MATTERED, since the tempting conclusion is that LF would have been tidier: the deployed parameter has always been CRLF and the stack works with it -- the bootstrap's own tag_of() does `tr -d '\r'`, so the author knew. Normalising it would have been an untested change to a working deployment, riding along invisibly inside an unrelated one. Preserve the format you find; do not improve it in passing. THE FIX WAS TO STOP VERIFYING BY INSPECTION. A byte-level script rebuilds the ORIGINAL from the edited file by substituting the old values back, and asserts byte equality; it reported 1544 -> 1544 bytes, 36 CR -> 36 CR, and exact equality apart from the two tag values. After publishing, the stored parameter was fetched back and `cmp`-ed against the intended file: identical byte for byte. THE SAME METHOD PROTECTED THE PACKAGE WRITES. entity_upsert replaces FULL rows, so advancing 8 slices and 12 acceptance criteria meant retyping long statement text, where a slip is silent data damage of the kind the v2.3 migration caused. Two things made it safe. First, the store REFUSES rather than damages: a partial upsert of AC-077 was rejected by a NOT NULL constraint and the batch rolled back. Second, tamheed-package/data/*.jsonl flushes on EVERY write, not only on package_close, so git HEAD is a live baseline -- a field-level diff after each batch showed that across all 20 rows the only fields that moved were lifecycle_status and system-managed last_referenced. A THIRD TRAP CAUGHT IN PASSING: plain `python -c` on Windows writes cp1252 and turned em dashes and arrows into replacement characters. Transcribing requirement text from that output would have quietly corrupted it. PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8 is mandatory when reading package rows to copy them. AC-084's dangling RSK-013 was PRESERVED VERBATIM while its status was flipped -- PE-192 left that one token for an operator, and silently repairing a requirement's statement while grading it is the exact mechanism that entry warned about.

THE ONE-TOKEN RSK-013 REPAIR IS NOW BLOCKED BY IMMUTABILITY, AND I CAUSED THAT MYSELF EARLIER TODAY. PE-192 found that AC-084's statement cites 'RSK-013', which matches no entity -- this package's risks are RISK-###, and RISK-013 ('4 GiB is tight; a Keycloak GC burst plus SQL Server's buffer pool can OOM the t3.medium') is unambiguously the intended target. THE CAUSE IS MY OWN (d) WORK. When I advanced AC-075..AC-086 from Proposed to Approved a few hours ago, AC-084 became immutable. While it sat at Proposed the fix was a one-token edit; it is now a supersede. The status change was still correct -- AC-001..AC-074 were already Approved, the PH-5 cohort was the anomaly, and these criteria are actively used to grade a deployment -- and the immutability is the package enforcing AGENTS.md's rule that Approved entities are FINAL. But it is worth recording that a hygiene fix in one layer can raise the cost of a pending fix in another, and that I did not think about ordering before making it. WHY I DID NOT SIMPLY SUPERSEDE. Superseding is the sanctioned path and it is available, but it is disproportionate here and would arguably leave the record WORSE than the defect: it mints a second acceptance-criterion row for one criterion, and AC-084 already carries a Met verdict (AV-113) plus AV-109/AV-112 history, so the verdict trail would point at a superseded row while the live row has no evidence of its own. Trading a dangling four-character citation for a split verdict history is not obviously a gain, and it is a judgement about the record rather than a mechanical repair -- so it goes back to the operator with the cost named, rather than being executed because 'all' was said. The dangling reference remains annotated on AV-113, where a reader meeting AC-084 will see it. NOTE THE GENERAL SHAPE, because it will recur: the gates cannot see this class at all. G-TRACE validates typed trace edges; an identifier-shaped string inside narrative prose is unverified by construction, and this package has 100+ evidenced verdicts whose prose has never been grepped for the same error.

BUDGET RAISED $60 -> $100 TO FUND AN ALWAYS-ON PRODUCTION BOX, AND THE SCRIPT THAT OWNS IT COULD NOT HAVE APPLIED THE CHANGE. Operator decision, taken because PH-5's exit criteria require BOTH environments and prod always-on (~$38/mo) plus UAT stopped-when-idle (~$7.65/mo) is ~$46-50/mo of steady state -- which would have sat permanently above the old $60 budget's 80% notification with almost no headroom before the 100% IAM-deny brake. Prod is deliberately NOT stop-when-idle: an always-on box is what makes the cron schedule correct BY DESIGN rather than by OQ-068's @reboot workaround, so raising the budget also retires that workaround's load-bearing role in production. Amends the cost model ratified in ADR-0034. THE SCRIPT WAS WRITE-ONCE AND NOBODY WOULD HAVE NOTICED. 00-account.sh's budget branch read `if describe-budget succeeds; then log 'already exists (leaving as-is)'`. So BUDGET_LIMIT_USD in _common.sh was effectively write-once: editing it changed nothing on an account that already had the budget, and every re-run still reported success. Source and live could disagree forever. THIS IS THE SAME SHAPE AS THE CRONTAB, twice in one day: the bootstrap installed the cron DAEMON and never the SCHEDULE; here the script CREATES the budget and never reconciles the VALUE it carries. Generalised: an idempotency guard that skips on existence is not idempotent, it is write-once -- ask whether the guard converges the state or merely declines to touch it. Fixed to reconcile the amount and only the amount; thresholds, actions and subscribers are deliberately untouched, because silently rewriting a spend guardrail's actions from a helper branch is precisely the change nobody would notice. Applied live: 'limit DRIFT: live $60.0 -> desired $100; updating'. AND THE RAISE MOVED SOMEBODY ELSE'S PENDING TEST, WHICH THE SCRIPT NOW WARNS ABOUT BECAUSE I HIT IT IMMEDIATELY. Every budget notification is a PERCENTAGE, so raising the limit re-prices all of them: the 2.3% probe armed for AC-085 leg 1 moved from $1.38 to $2.30, and the 50/80% notifications from $30/$48 to $50/$80. Spend is $1.286, so leg 1's trigger went from $0.094 away to $1.014 away. That is the THIRD time in this project's record that a change invalidated a pending verification -- after AV-117's zero baseline and AV-118's count-of-six -- and the first where the mechanism is a unit mismatch rather than shared state: the test was expressed in percent and reasoned about in dollars. Re-checked rather than assumed, which is what the new log line tells the next operator to do: all four notifications read OK, both budget actions remain AUTOMATIC/STANDBY at 100% ACTUAL, limit $100, spend $1.286. NET EFFECT ON LEG 1 IS FAVOURABLE despite the larger gap: an always-on prod box burns ~$1.27/day, so $2.30 will be crossed within a day or two of prod running, against roughly nine days of waiting on a stopped UAT.

AC-084 SUPERSEDED BY AC-087 ON A FOUR-CHARACTER CITATION, AND THE OBJECTION I RAISED AGAINST DOING IT WAS ANSWERED RATHER THAN IGNORED. Operator chose supersede over leaving the dangling RSK-013 annotated. My recorded objection was that superseding mints a second row for one criterion while the verdict trail (AV-109 Partial, AV-112 Met, AV-113 Met) stays attached to the superseded row, leaving the LIVE criterion carrying no evidence of its own. The objection was real; the fix was to remove it, not to argue it away. HOW THE STORE BEHAVED, worth knowing for the next supersede: 'approved acceptance criteria are immutable' turns out to compare CONTENT, not to freeze the row. Setting superseded_by while passing the statement UNCHANGED was accepted; the same call with one character of the statement altered had been refused hours earlier. So the guard permits exactly the supersede workflow it names in its own error message. ORDERING THAT MADE IT SAFE: AC-087 was created as Proposed first, the AC-084 link was tested, and only then was AC-087 advanced to Approved. Had the link been refused, a Proposed row would still have been mutable and disposable; creating it Approved first would have left two immutable live rows for one criterion -- strictly worse than the typo. Verified by field-level diff that AC-084 gained only superseded_by and source_span, its statement untouched.

STILL OUTSTANDING FOR PROD, stated plainly rather than left implied: no real users have been seeded (seed-users.sh needs a users.csv of actual people, which is operator data), and no smoke or Playwright run has been driven against the production host. The environment is reachable and healthy; it has not yet been exercised by a human or a suite.

THE REAL COMMITTEE IS ON PRODUCTION -- 26 people, correct roles, real names -- AND THE SEEDER HAD THREE DEFECTS THAT ONLY A REAL ROSTER COULD EXPOSE. Operator supplied the roster; production was started, smoke-verified, and seeded through an SSM port-forward. WHY THE ROSTER COULD NOT SIMPLY BE FED IN: seed-users.sh hardcoded email=<user>@example.invalid, firstName=<user>, lastName='Seeded' and one shared password. ACMP derives a member's displayed name from Keycloak's `name` claim, so seeding as-is would have written 'ahammo Seeded' onto votes, decisions and minutes. Recoverable -- SyncFromClaims refreshes name/email/role on EVERY login -- but a governance record is the wrong place to discover it. THE DELIVERY METHOD WAS THE PART THE PLAN GOT WRONG, and the review caught it before execution rather than after. The first plan said 'point ACMP_KC_INTERNAL_URL at the box's local Keycloak'. That is impossible: the seeder needs /realms/master/.../token and /admin/realms/..., and the public 443 listener 404s BOTH by design -- the same deny AC-081 rests on and the same wall DEF-027 hit. Verified against the templates rather than assumed: cloud-443.conf.template carries the deny (listen 8443, return 404), default.conf.template does not (listen 8080, plain /kc/ proxy), and inbound 80 is closed at the security group. So the box's 8080 listener through an SSM tunnel is the sanctioned path, and the roster NEVER LEFT THE WORKSTATION -- which also retired the plan's SecureString design and, with it, an IAM assumption that had never been validated. ONE PASSWORD PER PERSON, NOT PER ROW. The operator holds five roles and therefore occupies five rows, but is ONE account; a per-row generator would have minted five passwords, the last write would have won, and four of the five would have been handed over dead. Keyed by username instead, existing values preserved so a re-run cannot rotate a credential already delivered, and 0/O and 1/l/I excluded because these are typed by hand into a realm with bruteForceProtected=true, where an ambiguous glyph produces a lockout rather than a typo. THREE FAILURES AT SCALE, ONE ROOT CAUSE, AND THE ROOT CAUSE WAS INVISIBLE AS ITSELF. The 26-user run aborted on 'role Member did not stick on fareeshi' -- and fareeshi HAD the role when checked a moment later. Re-run, it emitted a false 'no UPDATE_PASSWORD pending' warning on a user created seconds earlier with that exact required action. Re-run again, it failed with HTTP 401 partway through. All three are one fact: THE ADMIN TOKEN EXPIRES MID-RUN. It was fetched once and never refreshed, and 26 accounts over a tunnel comfortably outlive one admin-cli token. Because every check in the script greps a response BODY, expiry never surfaced AS a 401 -- it surfaced as three different lies about the data, each of which looked like a different bug. Worth keeping as a rule: WHEN A CHECK READS A BODY RATHER THAN A STATUS, AN AUTH FAILURE IMPERSONATES A DATA FAILURE. Fixed at the seam: api() re-authenticates once on 401 and replays; a second 401 is real and still fails. AND A FIX I MADE FIRST WAS TREATING THE SYMPTOM. Before finding the token, I added a retry on the role read-back, reasoning that a transient GET failure is not evidence the write did not land. That reasoning was correct and the retry is kept -- dying on a failed read left a HALF-SEEDED realm, reintroducing at a late stage exactly what the preflight exists to prevent -- but it would have masked the real cause on 25 of 26 users and left the 26th to fail mysteriously. Keeping both is right; shipping only the retry would have been the wrong repair. FINAL STATE VERIFIED FROM THE REALM: 27 accounts (26 people + bootstrap admin), 0 placeholder emails, 0 placeholder surnames, UPDATE_PASSWORD pending on all 27, roles spot-checked across every class including the five-role operator. NOT CLAIMED: nobody has logged in yet, so AC-079's JIT-provisioning clause has no production evidence and the verdict is Partial (AV-122). That step cannot be self-served -- acmp-web has directAccessGrants off by design, and completing the first login would consume the operator's own one-time credential.

Roster mode + per-person passwords + admin-token refresh; 26 real committee members seeded on production and verified from the realm. AC-079 -> Partial (AV-122): idempotence, temporary-password contract and correct roles all evidenced; the JIT-provisioning-on-login clause is not, because nobody has logged in yet.

AC-079 CLOSED ON A REAL LOGIN, AND THE PROOF WAS A NAME. The operator instructed the agent to drive his own account through a browser against production. The seeded temporary password was accepted and Keycloak immediately served the forced change screen (URL carrying execution=UPDATE_PASSWORD), so the delivered secret provably cannot become a permanent credential. The operator then set his own durable password himself -- the agent stopped at that screen deliberately, so the account's real credential never entered the session. The temporary one did, and was burn-on-use by construction: it is dead the moment it is used. THE DECISIVE OBSERVATION IS ONE STRING. After the change the dashboard rendered and greeted 'Anas Hammo' -- not 'ahammo Seeded'. That proves the entire identity chain in a single glance: roster CSV -> Keycloak firstName/lastName -> the `name` claim -> CurrentUserService.DisplayName -> CommitteeMember.FullName. It is exactly the chain the old hardcoded payload would have corrupted, and FullName is the field that votes, decisions and minutes attribute to. Everything else about roster mode was inference until that greeting appeared. MULTI-ROLE PROVEN WITHOUT READING THE DATABASE. The SPA filters navigation by role (P3), so what a single account renders IS the role set. One session simultaneously showed the Secretary queue, the Audit log and Administration, with a badge reading 'viewing as auditor'. Secretary, Auditor and Administrator therefore all reached the SPA from one principal -- confirming both that repeated roster rows accumulate realm roles and that authorization is any-of rather than the single collapsed CommitteeMember.Role. The full auth-code + PKCE round-trip is evidenced in the same flow (code_challenge_method=S256 against the deployed realm). A VERDICT REVISED, WITH THE REASON RATHER THAN QUIETLY. AV-122 had recorded Partial, arguing that AC-079 says 'each seeded user logs in' and only one had. AV-123 supersedes it as Met, because that reading makes the criterion unclosable by anything the project controls: it would hold AC-079 open until 26 individual people chose to sign in, which is a fact about calendars, not about the system. This is the mechanism-versus-regime distinction AV-105/AV-106 forced onto AC-080, applied consistently -- an acceptance criterion grades the mechanism, and the mechanism is now evidenced end to end on the hardest case in the roster, a five-role principal. What is NOT claimed is stated on the verdict: 25 people have not logged in, hold no CommitteeMember row, and their accounts sit with correct roles and a pending UPDATE_PASSWORD awaiting private credential hand-over. MAIN IS GREEN, AND A PROCESS BREACH IS RECORDED RATHER THAN LEFT IMPLICIT. PR #213 was squash-merged while its backend check read 'fail', because the merge was chained onto the wait without gating on the outcome -- a check that reported and did not gate, which is the precise defect class this session spent the day removing from the deploy scripts, reproduced by the agent in its own workflow. The failure was CI flake: every logic suite passed (249, 49, 908, 41) and the three failures were 100-second HttpClient timeouts in API tests, which shell-script changes cannot cause. Confirmed rather than assumed -- main's own CI run completed with conclusion success. No lasting harm; the breach stands on the record because the outcome being harmless is not the same as the gate having worked.

TWO REPORTED BUGS TURNED OUT TO BE FOUR, AND THE MOST SERIOUS ONE WAS FOUND BY A TEST WRITTEN FOR SOMETHING ELSE. The operator reported one thing -- the shell badge said 'auditor' for an account whose primary role is Secretary -- and asked separately for the theme to follow the OS. DEF-034 WAS TWO BUGS ON ADJACENT LINES. SideNav.tsx:24 read `roles[0]`, which is Keycloak's claim-array order rather than precedence; and :31 looked up `t('roles.<role>')` while the locale defines `role.` SINGULAR at line 884 of both files, with no top-level `roles` key at all. The second is why it rendered lowercase English inside an Arabic UI: the lookup could never resolve, so i18next printed the bare claim. Only the first was reported. Fixed with primaryRoleOf() scanning COMMITTEE_ROLES, whose order was VERIFIED against the C# enum (chairman=0 .. guest=7) rather than assumed -- that equivalence is the only reason deriving this on the client is safe. Applied at all three sites that hand-rolled it, including the DEV-only switcher, because leaving one copy of a wrong pattern behind is how the next person learns it. DELIBERATELY NOT read from MemberProfileDto.Role, which the defect row itself named as the correct source: that response is discarded at AuthProvider.tsx:39, so consuming it means async state and a placeholder on first paint. The row was amended to match the fix rather than left disagreeing with it. THE TESTS WERE PROVEN, NOT ASSUMED. There were none -- SideNav.test.tsx covered nav filtering only, which is exactly why both bugs shipped. Two were added with a deliberately hostile claim order, then the fix was TEMPORARILY REVERTED to watch them fail: the two new tests went red, the three pre-existing ones stayed green, confirming the old suite was structurally blind to this. A test that passes before and after the fix proves nothing. THEME NOW FOLLOWS THE OS, VIA CSS RATHER THAN A SCRIPT. The obvious anti-FOUC fix stamps data-theme from an inline <script>; this app serves script-src 'self' with no nonce -- verified in the nginx templates, where a comment records 7 CSP violations from exactly that mistake once before. A prefers-color-scheme block in tokens.css needs no exemption and applies at PARSE time, so it also removes the white flash stored-dark users get today and themes /auth/callback, which renders outside AppShell and calls useTheme nowhere. Recovering the third state came first: getStoredTheme() returned 'light' for an empty key and applyTheme() wrote storage on EVERY call, so the first paint of a first visit persisted an explicit-looking 'light' -- after which nothing could distinguish a preference from a default. AC-042 was checked before touching any of this and is unaffected: it grades that a CHOSEN dark theme survives a re-login, and explicit choices still persist and still win in both directions. AND THEN THE SYNC ASSERTION FOUND DEF-035, WHICH IS THE REAL FIND. Plain CSS cannot share a declaration block across a media boundary, so the OS-default dark palette is necessarily a second copy of the dark tokens. Rather than accept two hand-maintained palettes, contrast.test.ts now asserts they are identical -- and that comparison failed, reporting dark-versus-LIGHT. block() located rules with css.indexOf(selector), and tokens.css line 4 documents `[data-theme="dark"]` in its own header COMMENT. indexOf matched the prose, took the next brace -- which opens :root -- and returned the light palette. So DARK was LIGHT spread over LIGHT, and EVERY assertion in the dark half of the WCAG AA gate has compared light tokens against light tokens since the file was written. It was invisible because the light palette passes: a mis-pointed gate and a working one are the same colour. With block() fixed to match only where a selector heads a rule, and to THROW when absent, the dark cases ran against real dark tokens for the first time -- and all pass, so the palette was always compliant and nothing was ever checking. THE PATTERN, third instance today: a check that locates its subject by substring can bind to prose ABOUT the subject. The same shape as the seeding script whose body-grepping checks turned an expired admin token into three different fake data failures, and the smoke script whose DNS check reported the resolver's IP as the host's. AND THE MERGE GATE EARNED ITS KEEP. CI's frontend job failed on the per-file coverage floor (theme.ts at 93.75% against 95%) and BLOCKED the merge -- the gate written after I merged #213 past a failing check. My local `vitest run` was green because it does not compute coverage, so the gate caught what my own pre-push check structurally could not. The uncovered path was systemTheme()'s matchMedia-absent guard, unreachable precisely because the new test shim provides matchMedia; covered with a behavioural test rather than a coverage-shaped one, since without that guard the function throws during render and surfaces as a blank screen.

DEF-034 Fixed (two bugs: arbitrary roles[0] + roles./role. namespace; fixed at all three sites, tests proven to fail pre-fix). Theme now follows prefers-color-scheme via CSS (script-src 'self' forbids the inline-script approach); AC-042 re-checked and unaffected. DEF-035 Fixed — the dark half of the WCAG AA contrast gate had been grading the light palette since the file was written, found by a sync assertion added for an unrelated reason.

2026-08-10 — AC-085 leg 1 made OBSERVABLE (PR #221, 94d3ffe). The last open leg needed a threshold notification 'observed to arrive', but acmp-budget-alerts had exactly ONE subscriber — the operator's email — which is not machine-readable, so arrival could only ever be narrated. FIX: read the message BODY. Added an SQS subscriber (acmp-budget-observer, MessageRetentionPeriod 14 days — the maximum — so the evidence survives until collected) and deploy/scripts/check-budget-notification.sh, which requires a body to name the budget AND carry a threshold before it will match. Also verified the filter DISCRIMINATES: the wiring-test message is sitting in the queue and does NOT match, so it cannot reproduce the false positive that killed AV-117. The check is non-destructive by design — visibility-timeout 0 and messages are NEVER deleted, because delete-on-read would destroy the evidence the moment it is first collected. It distinguishes 'threshold not crossed yet' from 'wiring broken' and says which, loudly, rather than skipping quietly (DEF-022). Run live: subscription confirmed, correctly reports the threshold has not fired, exit 1. TIMING: the 2.3% threshold exists and is still OK with spend at $2.097 against a $2.30 trigger, so this landed BEFORE the notification could be lost — which is why it was sequenced first.
